THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Interviewer: Stanley Dance

Oral History -- Eddie Durham
Sides 1-2

Washington, D. C.
August, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
Now we're testing, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. And today we're recording Eddie Durham.
When were you born, Eddie?
And nine.
Yeah, but they got six. I was going to let it stay like that. It was a credit.
But it was really 1909.
They got 1906 in all the books they got on that.
So it should be 1909.
1909, but everybody -- seemed like they --
Well, we'll put three years on it.
What do you think, we should stick to that 1906?
No, if 1909 is your +-
They seem to think it's quite a novelty. That's because (unintelligible.)
19th of August.
That's right.
And this was in San Marcos, Texas.
In San Marcos, yeah.
How big a town was that? In those days?
Very small population, maybe 1,000 or two, maybe not that much.
What did they do there?
Well, when I was born, I was so young. I don't know what -- I don't have no idea what was going on. Mostly farming around, I think. Yeah, I think it was farming and cattle.
Yeah.
A lot of Spanish people, that spoke strictly Spanish.
What did your father do?
He was a farmer and bronco, break wild horses and --
Oh, yeah?
And a terrific fiddle player.
Oh.
Yeah, those were his specialties.
What sort of fiddle would he play?
Turkey in the Straw, that kind of stuff. Play for dances.
Yeah. And was your mother musical?
No, no. All the brothers was, and --
Oh, you had -- how many brothers did you have?

Well, I had three, outside of myself. And the other ones was my cousins. And so everybody thought they were brothers, so they just growed up in our family, too. All their people deceased. There was Clyde and Allen and all those ones that they --
Which was the younger one? Clyde was the one --
No, Roosevelt, my real brother, the piano player.
That was your real brother.
Yeah.
The others were cousins?
He was the baby, yeah.
Oh, I see. Earl was a cousin.
No, Earl's a brother, and he's a terrific clarinet and saxophone player. That's the only thing I (inaudible).
And Roosevelt was in --
In piano.
Piano.
Yeah.
And what about that Allen?
Allen was a trombone player.
He was your brother?
No, cousin.
Cousin. And Joe?
Brother.
He played bass, right?
Bass, yeah. He's the one that was with Calloway.
And Clyde? He played bass?
Bass, too. He played the tuba.
And who was Sylvester?
Sylvester, he was a cousin, but he wasn't raised up in the family.
Oh.
He wasn't raised in the family like those others.
Well, how come they --
I don't know how Sylvester got in the picture.
Oh, well, I guess somebody heard of him somewhere.
Yeah.
How come they all played bass?

Well, my oldest brother, he played a trumpet, see. And he could double off from one to the other. So Clyde only played the bass, but my oldest brother was a violin player, a trumpet player, and he played all instruments. In fact, he taught me from the beginning.
The oldest is Roosevelt.
No, the oldest was Joe.
Oh, the oldest was Joe. Yes, I got you.
And Earl was the next brother.
Yeah.
Then myself, and then Roosevelt.
Yeah.
And the cousins was in between us.
Yeah, yeah. So do you have like a family band?
Yeah, we always had a family band playing a lot, in school and everywhere.
Well, I mean, what did you do, play gigs at weekends or what?
Weekends, take gigs and like that,yeah. We had the whole band except drums, and we always used an outside drummer.
Now, when Joe taught you, what did he teach you?
He taught me on the trombone and the guitar because he could play all instruments.
I see.
And he was -- at that time he was with the 101 -- not the 101, 24th Infantry, which merged with the Tenth Cavalry and he was in that setup, the guards for Teddy

Roosevelt. Of course, he was much older than me because we had a lot of family between us, and he was stationed out there, and I would go out there when I was young, and that's when he would teach me, because in those days it was nothing but light guard duty, like the National Guards, and you had plenty of time. He'd take me out, then he got me a place to stay right near the camp and he would teach me music, you know, when I wasn't in school.
He was teaching me to play, you know, to a degree.
But which did you really get on first, then, trombone or guitar?
They both come along about together.
Oh.
Right about together, because we kept a lot of instruments. Start right on one, play one for awhile (inaudible).
So you really --

Yeah, started both of them, yeah, both of them. I had them all the time. Played four string, and I kept a banjo. In fact, I have a picture now down there that I made with the banjo and the four-string and the trombone. I have that picture.
Oh, you have?
Yeah, and it's marked on the back, 1927, and Battles is on that picture.
Battle ________ ?
Is on that picture, too, with all the instruments. And we played nine instruments, three of us.
I'd like to see that.
That was Battles and myself and another.
Were you in the band?
Yeah, we had a small band.
No, but, I mean, when this picture was taken. Well, we'll come to that later, won't we?
Yeah, well, what was happening, we just make it with the brass section.
Yeah.
We played nine instruments.
Well, when do you sort of begin to play professionally, out of the family band?

That's when I went with -- well, it was one incident left out there, which was Doug Morgan's dramatic show. That's when I travelled with four brothers. And just before -- in between there, just before I got involved with (inaudible).
Keep your voice up a bit.
Yeah, well, we travelled with that -- called Doug Morgan Dramatic Show. It was a white show, but he had the black guys in the band, see. That's it, he had a
black band. So that's when I played the guitar, and he bought me my first guitar.
Yeah.
Because I'd always borrow them and use them, borrow and travel and give it back. He bought the first guitar for me, which was a four-string. I was playing trombone and guitar in his show.
This was before you went with the 101 Ranch?
Yeah, that was before, yeah. Battles, I think, was on the Doug Morgan show, too. And then we -- yeah, and then we went to the 101 Ranch.
Well, now, explain what that was, actually.
The 101 Ranch?
Yeah. I mean, they had a circus.
It was a big circus, with -- like the Ringling Brothers Show, only they had a bigger ring, because in some of the acts they had three or four tribes of Indians.
Oh?

And Chief White Horse, Chief White Cloud and they'd perform just like they do in a movie. And they'd have a big arena with a lot of hay, and the settlers would come out in three or four wagons with the canvass, and the Indians would ride out on the horses, maybe 15 or 20 of
then, with arrows.
It was a Wild West show.
Yeah, and sometimes rifles. And they had blanks, and the settlers would shoot and the Indian would fall off his horse, and all that, just like the movies, they could ride those horses.
This was outdoors, not in the tent?
No, that was in the tent. Be setting way around and they'd be out in the arena, like, where the people could sit and look, just like a stadium.
Oh, I see.
Because the last show that I was with them, was at the Yankee Stadium in New York.
Oh.
And then they tore down that year after that. They went to Europe with that show.
How long were you with them?
Stayed with them two seasons, I believe.
How long would the season be?
The warm weather.
Hm?
You know, as long as the weather was warm, right up until --
It would be a summer thing.
Yeah, that's what it was, because they
couldn't do it in the cold.
But where would you go?
They played everywhere. We played Detroit --
Oh, all over the States.

Yeah, and they set it up out in the and they had two big bands. They had a great big band and they had about 15 pieces of black band, and then they'd break the black band down to about nine pieces for the minstrel show at night.
Yeah.
They had a big minstrel show, see, like.
So, really, -- but when you were playing -- there were two bands, were there?
Two bands.
Well, what was the difference between the black and the white band?
The white band, see, they'd parade every day.
Oh.
And the big white band would play for the parade, and then later on the minstrel band would be further back in the parade playing jazz type of stuff.
Yes, I see.
With the minstrel show. The comedians on the wagon. It was two different types of shows.
I see. Yes, I see.
In a certain part of the night, they'd break and have the minstrel show.
Yeah.

So that's about all they had. They had the Wild West and the minstrel show. Minstrel show consisted of about five or six fellows and five or six girls and about a nine-piece band on the stage. So that's how I got into the ranching deal.
Oh.
See.
Now, in this band, you were playing what, trombone?
I was playing trombone.
Yeah.
And at night, when they give a dance -- then I started giving dances myself, and then that's when I used the guitar.
Yes, I see.

See. And that's how I learned to voice above three-part harmony, because after the show break at 9:00 at night, we'd always go someplace where you could give a dance, charge 50 cents to get in, all the old guys play the French horn and all those things, they always was glad to get the chance to play some music I wrote.
How did you learn to arrange?
Well, my brother was teaching me to read.
Yes.
I learned to read a little, quite a bit. And then, he could write a little, then I started to try to voice. So in those days, they only used a triad, like, three-part harmony?
Yes.
So I figured, with my guitar I could find more than that.
Yes.

So I'd write it down and I'd say, well, you gotta rehearse to play tonight. And all the guys -- well, can I go, can I go, so I said, yeah, well, I want the other three trombones. So I would get four trombones together, and I'd experiment in voicing. And they didn't know the difference in the sound, so they just played what I had. And I learned that you could voice up to four and five part harmony.
Hadn't heard of -- I mean, in those days they didn't even have three trombones in band, did they?
No, they had -- it was four in that band, though, that I was playing in, see.
Yeah. But in those sort of -- in the early jazz groups, the trombones were sort of voiced with the
They was sort of voiced with the trumpets. When the trumpets got a little bit too swift, the trombones would (unintelligible) or something else to do, tailgate, they called it.
Yes, yes.

But in this case here, the musicians were terrific musicians in those bands. They were hand picked. Because they could play any of those overtures, anything, you know. So the way I set the band up as an orchestra, we didn't have no trap drums. I'd get the bass drummer just to play his bass drums, sit there and beat the bass drum.
Yeah.
And I'd get the trap drummer, one of the trap drummers, to come and play the trap. So two men was doing just what one guy does today. One would play the after beat --
Yes, I see. Yes.

And for the piano, I would get me two or three French horns, voice two or three part harmony for them, and just let them play the after beat just like a piano would play, they'd use a lot of that. So that would give that piano sound. And we didn't have any saxophone players in the band. But later on had clarinets, I'd take the clarinets and do reed work.
Now, when you were doing this, these would be guys from the white band as well?
If we'd run short, I'd get a couple of white guys. It didn't make any difference, they all wanted --
Well, how big was the black band?
The black band was about 14 pieces.
Well, where would you get four trombones from, out of that?
Well, see, I was doubling.
Yeah.
And then I'd get a couple of guys from the white band.
Yes, I see.
Because they had -- no, that band was bigger than that, because they had three trombone players.
Well, there you go.
Yes, they did.
Yeah.
Four trumpets -- no, they must have had a much bigger band than that.
Well, what sort of music did you play? I mean, with the minstrel show you'd sort of play kind of Ragtime ranky-time stuff.
Kind of ragtime, but it wasn't too jazzy.
No, but then, when you were marching,
No, we'd play from the march books then.
You would.
Yeah. And the only way they got away from it, I think I had something I wrote up there once.
Yeah.
And it was a blues, and that turned the tide over there.
Well, what kind --
But we was on the wagon, then.
Yeah.
See, and I could play a little blues from the wagon, you know.
Yeah. Well, what sort of year are we talking about with this?
That must have been around 1921, somewhere around in there.
I see.
That's when I left the circus. They went to Europe from here. I played at Yankee Stadium and I didn't go any further.
Did the black band go to Europe?
They probably -- yeah, I think so, yeah. I think they did. I'm not sure.
Well, --
I'm not sure.
Who would you have heard in those days, I mean, sort of what jazz people would you have heard?
We had a terrific trumpet player there named Amos White. John Mason, from -- who was the leader. Those guys could do anything with a trumpet.
Yeah.

See, but they never played in the dance bands, see. They only played -- the other seasons, they just laid back and go with those shows, went out with them older fellows. And we had a terrific drummer there. But they, --
But, at this time you hadn't heard Louis Armstrong or King Oliver or anybody like that?
No, I heard Louis Armstrong right after that. I went to Chicago and heard him playing with King Oliver.
You did?
Yeah, they played a ballroom and it cost about 50 cents to get in, so I didn't have any money, and I was one of the younger guys that would line up on the windows, listening.
How did you get to Chicago, with this Ranch?
Yeah, I went to Chicago with the Ranch. Battles was with me, then. I went to Chicago, and then
I went back, and I stayed there. I was around about 21 then, I guess, and I went to school a little while there.
Well, wait a minute, if you were 21, that makes -- that brings you up to 1921.
I was pretty close to it, if I wasn't. I was a kid, I know.
Well, 1909, that would bring you to 1930, if you were born in 1909.
Yeah. I don't remember the year, but --
I mean, if Louis was with --
Let me see, now. I was in Chicago -- yeah, Louis was with King Oliver Arthur. That's where I heard him, in a ballroom there, in an old dance ballroom.
Well, that's about 1922.
Might have been. I ain't got the exact year on that. I don't know exactly how old I was then.
But, anyway, you heard him there.

That's where I heard him and I started working in a bakery shop called Starkey's Bakery, a German bakery. And that was a big concern, and that's where I was living to play this music. So I was studying with the U.S. School of Music, which my brother told me to find it. Because I was a rounder, you know.
Well, --
I might have been younger than that.
Well, I was thinking, and what sort of money would you get with that, when you were with that band?
The circus?
With the 101 Ranch Band. What would they pay you?
I think you got -- I must have been getting about $25 a week.
Which was quite a good bit of money in those days.
Yeah, well, the guys was up in the money then, those guys that could read anything. I was getting about $25 a week, room and board and everything.
Room and board paid for, in addition to --
Yeah. When you go in the circus, everything else is ______, too.
Well, I mean, the $25 was quite a lot of money.
Yeah, maybe $20, $25, around there. Yeah.
In those days.
I was rich when payday come. But a lot of other guys was up in the $40's and $50's.
Yeah. But even so, I mean, if you came to Chicago as a kid, you'd probably save some money.
Oh, I had -- yeah, put it right in the bank.
Yeah. So how long did you stay there?
In Chicago?
Yeah.

About a year or two. I'm trying to remember where I went when I left there. That's when I really went into the business heavy. Went from there on into Kansas City. But what I want to say about this band -- I don't want to jump the subject.
Well, we can --

They didn't march and play. They had big wagons for it, the big band wagons, the big band. There was about 30 pieces in that big white band, see. And they played on a truck and then we come along last with the minstrel show, with a few comedians on it, and that's -- see, we could play Sweet Georgia Brown if we wanted to, anything we wanted to play. But the guys didn't know much jazz.
No.
So I wrote up a couple of things for them, made one of them jazz licks on the trombone and --in the street and it just come down, you see.
Yeah. These trucks, were they dragged by horses or were they motors?
By horses.
Oh, dragged by horses.

Yeah, horses. They had a million horses, elephants, and everything else. Sometimes the wagon would break down. One elephant would come and push the whole wagon out. I was telling somebody about that the other day. Ten horses pulled, one elephant that was called Big Jimbo, just push it out of the --
How did they move the circus in those days?
They had their own train cars, lots of long train cars.
So all of these trucks and things had to be loaded on the train?
Yeah, and they had the wild animals also, snakes, lions.
Must have been a pretty big job, that.
Yeah, it was a big show. It was bigger than Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey because it had to be because they had the wagons and horses and a lot of shooting and all that.
Yeah.
Trick shooting and everything. What went on in the movies, that's what went on right there.
So -- but, actually, for somebody our of Marcos, Texas, I guess this seemed like the life, didn't it?
Yeah. I was just hard to handle, that's all, I was so young.
No, but, I mean, you really found it exciting, I guess.
Yeah, but, you see, I learned something I didn't think would do any good. I learned to voice music up to five and six part harmony right there, from that.
Yeah.

And when I got out, and went to the Benny Morton band, that's where the trouble started. Because they were using three-part harmony, and we got Lips Page to come in, so like the chord or the tonic third and the fifth, I added in the sixth. And the band didn't want to hear that. They'd say, that's out of tune, no.
Too rich for them.

Yeah, they said it's too rich. So I said, let Lips play the sixth. We'll never give it to any of the others because they didn't want to hear it. But Benny says, I don't care what it sounds like, play what he writes. And that's when Morton Swing came in, too, while Benny was in the band. And --
Well, actually,when you listen to the old records by that band, that was a pretty poor band.
Yeah.
I mean, it really -- it wasn't until
you and Lips Page and people got in it that it started to sound like something.
Yeah, because they had the old style. Three saxophones and two trumpets and one trombone, and they would double the notes.
Yeah.

So they wanted to know who was going out of the band when they bring somebody else, he's gotta be going to play my note. And that was an argument, say, you're trying to find somebody. I'd say Lips is not going to play anybody's note. He's going to play his own note. And every time they'd play in rehearsal and break for intermission, they all wanted to see Benny, without me. They'd get in a corner, talking -- Benny, the guy's out of his mind, that don't sound right, that chording and all that stuff.
So -- but, now, that's a funny thing. Now when I got ready to put my note in, we had five brass then, see, and I played valve trombone a lot.
Oh, did you play valve?
Yeah, I didn't never say anything, but that's valve trombone I played with Benny's band, mostly.
And --
Well, of course, you could execute on that.
Yeah, you see, and I could play high.
Yeah.
I could hit those trumpets.
I mean, that was why Duke had Juan Toosaw (PHONETIC), wasn't it?
Yeah, maybe so.
I mean, early on, I mean, he could --
Play his movements. So -- but, in other words, when I added in the fifth, which was the ninth chord, that sounded pretty to them.
Yeah.

The sixth, they didn't get used to it too quick. But the five part, they did. So we got along with the band nice like that. But I already had the experience from that circus, because the guys with them trombones would make any note I'd say. That was just -- they were sitting around and playing cards and gambling, they'd love to come down there and rehearse.

So we'd divide up the money, we'd play for a little money, four or five dollars apiece. And I liked that, playing for the crowd. We'd play til 11:00, most every night I'd get left in town, so they always left a ticket for me.
Well, now, when -- let's just check on this again. According to this book, after the 101, you worked with Ed Dixie Ramblers. Is that right?
Yeah, that was with 101 Wild West
Circus, with Mamie Smith. That was a big show.
Oh, another show.
Yeah, that was a 7-11. They had about 70-some people on that show.
They didn't do -- that wasn't a circus now?
No, that was -- we left the -- and we went to that show. Now, that's when Battles was kind of shining with the band.
Yeah.
So the last engagement we played was at the Orphan Theatre, I believe, in Newark, New Jersey, and that's when the show started.
Oh, you went all over with that show, too.
Went all over the country with that show.
Well, how big a band was Battles' band in that --

That was -- let me see. Three saxaphones. Herschel Evans was in that band. We went and got him. You know, he was a cousin of mine, from Los Pasos, Texas. And he was playing alto, so we put him on tenor. And it was three saxophones and Battles was on trumpet and somebody -- it must have been about a nine-piece band.
I see. Was Battle playing much trumpet in those days?
Yeah, he was playing trumpet in those days.
How good was he in those days?
He was a good trumpet player.
Was he?
Yeah, he was a good trumpet player. Because they didn't do much Roy Eldridge type of stuff in those days.
No.

They just played, you know. You had to have some melody, and he could execute. But always could write much more than what I ever wrote for any band. But it didn't make sense for me to stretch out and ________ anything on the paper. I always wrote what I thought the band could play.
Yeah.
I've never really stretched out with what I could do. I doubt if Duke ever did.
But this band of Battles, nine pieces, you had to play for the show, though.
We played the show, in the pit.
So --
In the pit.
Well, I mean, in other words, you had to be pretty good musicians to --
Oh, yeah, we had to read.
Yeah, yeah. But did you do any sort of an act as a jazz fan --
With the show?
Yeah.
Yeah, well, the band had to open as an overture, you know.
Yeah, but, I mean, I wondered whether with this band you were getting more into jazz than before.
Yeah, yeah, smoothen it up, yeah.
Yeah.
Smoothing it up.
Anybody else in in that I would know besides Herschel Evans?
There was nobody in that but my brothers. The one on the piano was there, and the clarinet player was there. Joe and Earl and Roosevelt and myself, all four of us were there.
Well, you weren't all four in the 101, were you?
No, just myself, Battles and my oldest brother. He was playing trumpet there.
In the show.
Yeah, he played trumpet.
In the 101.
In the 101.
But in this -- what is this one called that we're talking of now? Which show is this?
This is the 7-11, with Edgar Battle.
Yeah, and here there were four brothers.
Yeah, we were there together.
Yeah.
Yeah, til it broke up. And that was a big show from New York.
Yeah.
It was Mamie Smith's show, 7-11, by the Goldberg Brothers.
Now, what do you reckon this would be? See, Mamie Smith made that big record there, in -- when was it she made it?
It must have been before that, because I don't remember really recording with her.
No, you didn't record, but I think what made Mamie Smith big was when she --
Maybe she made the record before.
When she had that hit record, I think that's when they started sending her all over the country. Her first record was in 1920, so that would be about right. This
would be about 1921.
Yeah.
But what I'm really trying to fit in is, when it was that you went to Chicago. I don't think that could have been after the 101 Ranch.
Well, maybe --
But it could be this coming year. After you played with Battles' band. See, Louis was out there in '22.
I think I was in Chicago before I went with that show, yeah.
But when you stayed in Chicago, it was to go to this music college, was it?

Yeah, I went there, because my brother knew a doctor there named Dr. Dorsey, and I lived with Dr. Dorsey, he owned a drugstore. And then from -- I worked a little at the lunch counter and I would go down to this trade school. You'd work your way through it, and I worked in the bakery shop for awhile.
Well, what did you learn in this school?

A little bit more about -- well, I would say dynamics and correct wording for this and that, because they were using a lot of Latin terms, you know, like -- they was using a lot of Latin terms in music, like tempo and -- wait a minute, I forgot the words.
Well, Italian terms.
Yeah, Italian --
Accelerando, and --
Yeah.
-- all that stuff.
Poca tempo and all that stuff.
Yeah.

Yeah. So finally I got away from all that. And so that's what I learned there. It got so they couldn't offer me much and (unintelligible) what I got here, I got a foundation, so I went creating for myself. So when I came to New York, that's when I run into guys like Bingie Madison, who was voicing, and then ran into Don Redman, and Don Redman was doing six-part harmony, and that's when -- and when I heard his (unintelligible) I said, what do you name this chord? He says, it's just a double the minute. Nobody's even named it yet. You get that six part.

So, now I got some things where you can do seven-part harmony and that sounds all right, but you need instrumentation to do it. So I made one for Battles with his six saxes, top to bottom, all six-part harmony, commercial melody. That was about three years ago, it's still in the books.
Well, actually, of course, in a way, the bands weren't ready for this, were they?
No. I mean, they couldn't even hear it.
I mean, they couldn't read it, they couldn't -- there were almost too many people who couldn't read well.
Yeah, and even if they'd read the note they didn't hear well.
No.
They could only hear the triad.
Yeah, yeah. Well, that's what was in their head.

But now they can hear anything, guys here -- augmented flats, 18 fifths and everything now. They know just what you're doing. And that was a little edge I had on them with the Basie band, (inaudible) was in the band. They say, we hear a peculiar sound in this reed section in that background. That's when I used to use organ harmony a lot, because you can dissolve odd sounds, and I'd always tell Earl, say, look make this a flat fifth. I'd say, but I don't want to put the accidentally in front of it, because -- like, you know how in this place, guys (inaudible) trying to see, what was that note I heard in there when he was holding that chord?
Yeah.
They'd look at it and do this, and everybody would laugh. You could tell --
Yeah.
But what it was, if it was a F flat,
F sharp, and it would be an F flat the way he'd make it, but I wouldn't let him put the signature there.
Well, because everybody was stealing.
Yeah, they didn't know how to -- they'd say, oh, sure can bend those notes. So that's one of the tricks. I always did have an idea. I like to create.
Yeah.
And Duke, I don't know that much about him, but I know enough to know, he liked to create, and Don Redman.
Yeah.
So if you didn't hold him down with his own thing, he probably went on out in space because he wanted to hear something else.
Yeah, but he liked the (inaudible), too.

So you had to -- (inaudible) had to stop him to hold him back, was what we could do, because there wasn't no limit to where he could go. So that's Stan Kenton's idea, too. He'd keep on going if he could get by with it.
Well, after this period with Edgar Battle, what do you think happened then?
Battles went with Georgia's White Bryant, or either Willie Pratt or somebody.
Now, that's a good bit later.
Yeah.
But I was wondering what you did.
Oh, I know what you mean.
You said you played with Eugene Coit, Jesse Stone.
I think I went back to Kansas City, yeah, something like that. And then I played with -- I stayed in Kansas City around -- before I joined Benny Morton, I was there in Kansas City a couple of years.
Oh, yeah, well, I mean, I've got you with -- they've got you listed as playing with Gene Coin, Jesse Stone --
Well, that was in Oklahoma.
Teaholder -- T. Holler
Teaholder was in Kansas City.
And Walter Page's Blue Devils.
Yeah. I didn't stay within those bands long enough, though. Maybe just a few weeks. And when I left the Blue Devils, I went to Benny Morton.
Yeah, but --
Somewhere in there.
-- there's a good few years here.
I guess. But, anyway, I say, I knew where the good musicians are. Well, I'd say, get some of the Blue Devils, so that's how we got the Blue Devils. We got Walter Page in there and --

But, you know, I mean, we're talking really of probably 1922, and we've got -- let's see, you don't get with Benny Morton -- oh, Morton you get with in 1929. And -- well, do you remember anything about Gene Coin's band?
Yeah, that was in Shiny, Oklahoma, the Blueglass Ballroom.
Oh, yes.
For the Frederick Brothers, who come to New York for awhile, who I got (inaudible) buddies when they moved here. So, Gene Coin's Black Aces, that's who that was, and Clyde was with the band.
Clyde.
Era. Trombone player.
Oh, yeah, yeah,
Not Clyde, Alan Era. Yeah, Clyde was there, too, both of them.
Alan was the trombone player.
Yeah, and Clyde was playing bass, and that's how I think they got me in there.
Yeah.

Yeah. But, otherwise, Stanley, when I was in Kansas City, there's something missing, because that was about a year or six months ago I was with Chauncy Don's Rinky Dinks. That was about the next best band in Kansas City.
Whose band?
Chauncy Don.
How do you spell that?
C-h-a-r-n-c-y D-o-n, Charny Don.
I don't know that name.
No, nobody did. He was a terrific leader.
What did he play?
He was just director.
Oh.

But you know who was with that band, was Eddie Tompkin, Paul Weston, because we formed a clique, which was the two trumpets and myself and Budd Johnson -- I mean, and Keg Johnson. And a guy named -- I can't think of his name, there was five of us. That's when we all went into Jesse Stone's band, the same way.
I see.
And every summer, Paul and Eddie got out of the school, they would go to Buffalo and play with ____. So that's why ____ was always trying to get me, because we already had a brass section in town.
Ah, yes. Well, this Chauncy Don?
Yeah.
Was he a musician or just a sort of front man?
I forgot now. He was a front man
because we had terrific musicians in that center.
Where did you play?
Played right in Kansas City, club dates. Just like (inaudible).
Must have been a good band, though. I mean, those people were better than Benny Morton.
Yeah, because they could execute more. Yeah, Paul Weston and I, we could play it free.
Yeah. Were any of your brothers in that band?
No, just myself and King Johnson, played -- wherever the one was, the other one was there, and then them three trumpets. So we went to Jesse Stone with the same brass section.
Yes.
And we liked Jesse because Jesse would throw anything on the paper and we liked that.
Yeah, I was going to say, he was -- as an arranger, he was ahead in those days, wasn't he?
Yeah, he's -- today, Jesse Stone is so underrated.
He's still alive.
Yeah, I heard him about two years ago. He's playing with a ______, he and his wife. He's playing a little organ, she's playing a drum, and they go out here
and play. They played holiday and motels a lot. They got some act. Both of them are singing duos and singing.
He's a --
All his old tunes and --
He's a piano player.
Yeah. He wrote Hidey-Ho and numbers like that.
You think he's a good piano player or just a sort of arranger's piano --
He's an arranger's piano and also a background man for the band (inaudible) the band.
Oh, yeah. It's surprising that nobody ever gets on him for -- I mean, maybe he should do one of these things, because he must be nearly --
(Inaudible) we play a song every night, Hidey-Ho and -- even Frank Williams got that when was on it. And he did a lot of other songs. Wait a minute. He did Hucka Buck and a lot of other things.
But this band he had was really a very good one at that time, wasn't it?
Yeah, yeah. Ten years ahead.
You were playing trombone in it.
Yeah.
Well, where does Teaholder come in?
Teaholder had Andy Kurtz' band.
Kirk
Yeah, before Andy Kurtz.
Yeah, and then I went in there, just a little while, may not be over two or three weeks. And Teaholder run off and left the band. Now, some run away with him.
Yeah, there was a story about running off with the money or something.
Well, he was the type that would go off with the money.
Yeah, I've heard that.
They wouldn't let him come back in anymore, and then Andy Kurt took the band. They gave it to Andy. And I didn't stay very long.
Was that a cooperative band?
All those bands were.
They all were.
Well, when they were -- I mean, what did that mean, that the leader took just a little extra?

Well, I tell you how it went with the Benny Morton band. They promote their own dances. He'd rent a big hall like the agents do now. He'd go down and rent a big auditorium. And they'd write themselves. He'd get some men on the door and put out some publicity. And when night come, when they'd divide the money up, any expenses --
Take the expenses out.
They got any expenses, --
Yeah.
And then they'd divide the money.
But, I mean, -- do you mean to say that Benny Morton didn't get more than --
No more than the fellows.
Well, why was that? That doesn't seem --
He thought that the men was worth just the same thing he was. Any musician in his band, he felt like a musician side man was worth the same thing as the leader.
Yeah, but you'd have thought -- well, of course, they took all the expenses out, but you would have thought that as leader he should have --
Had something for being leader.
Yes, and also, -- yeah, he should be, because, after all, you playing with your trombone sat down and played.
That's right.
But, now, he's got to play the piano and he's got to handle the business.

He'd run and handle the business and the and all of that, and you couldn't tell him anything else. He just -- well, I'll take out the expenses for what I did, I'm the leader, I'm supposed to go out and get it.
Well, he probably took care of himself in some respects.
Some -- yeah, something, because he --
Well, how did you come to get with the Blue Devils?
Probably through Buster Smith and Booker Pittman. I knew them when they had the band they called the Blue Moon Chasers.
Yeah.

Which was a good band, because they had Booker Pittman, (inaudible) and Buddy Johnson was in that band, Herschel, and when ______ went out, I think Buster Smith came in. And you hear them, you get with that band a little while and then -- let's go to the Blue Devils. You get hungry and you go to the Blue Devils.
Do you know why they called it the Blue Devils?
I never did know why, no.

Because there was an article recently in the paper called Grackel where Ralph Ellison, the writer, said that in the old days, during -- when they had range wars, the people used to go and cut the barbed wire fences were called Blue Devils. I wonder if you ever heard that?
I heard that, but I didn't know the band was connected with that.
Well, it just makes you wonder whether that's where Walter Page got his title from.
I believe they named these bands, like, the Clouds of Joy, and the Blue Devils, Gene Coin's Black Aces -- I believe they were referring to color complexion.
Yeah. Because, Blue Devils, you know --
They always wanted to let you know they was a black band.
Yeah.
They always named it something that --
The Clouds of Joy --

Dark Clouds of Joy. I don't know if that name was tied with it or not. See, the clouds are dark, clouds are joy, clouds are joy. Back in those days, clouds generally come -- they dark when it's going to rain and they never think about clouds.
Yeah.
But I think it was related to identifying themselves as a black band.
Well, yeah, I would imagine --
And I thought that's what the Aces were, the Black Aces, meaning the -- you know, the ace was the top card and that guy's an ace. I think that's what they referred to.
Yeah.
Ace was supposed to be the greatest thing that was, the top card.

Well, the only thing is, you know, Blue Devils is -- when you talk of having the blues, years -- I mean, way back, 300 or 400 years ago, they used to say that a person, if he felt sick or down or depressed, they've got a case of the blue devils.
I believe part of that was --
That could mean -- I mean, some of those old things --
They did go by those terms.
Yeah, I mean, there's a lot of hangovers from much further back in the past than we sometimes are aware of, you know.
Yeah.
Well, where had you met Buster Smith?
Dallas, Texas.
Yeah? What were you doing there when you met him?
I was living in Terro, going to school 30 miles.
Oh.
It was a musical school, see.
Oh, so you -- this is another --
That was a musical school. They had a

teacher there named Professor Barnett, and it was one of them schools out there where the principal, anything he wanted to do, the whites backed it. So he had school, he had everything going on in that school.
Oh, yeah?

All kind of -- he had the best band in Texas in that school there. And the best of the musicians came out of that band. And so I was always active with the music. So I used to go to Dallas, 32 miles, go over there on Sundays with a girl and ride, you know, things like that. And that's how I met Buster Smith and I started playing with him. We played dances with some of the little groups, even with Buster's little band.
Now, Buster had a band, did he?
Yeah, he had a band, too, had a little band there.
Well, now, he was a well-schooled musician.
To me, he was the greatest.
Well, where did he get this stuff from? I mean, how --
Himself.
Huh?
I think he was self-taught.
Self-taught?
Yeah, like Herschel.
Oh, I wondered, because he always sounded --
He writes a lot now.
Yeah, but it sounded as thought he were a little better schooled than the average guy.
Yeah, yeah. Well, he got into it later, and you can teach yourself from books and --
Yeah, of course, yeah.
-- experience.
But not everybody has that kind of mind, where you go and buy books or get books.

When we made this Kansas City story, he bought a -- brought a trunk of blues music. And some of that stuff, you never realize it needs to be on the market. I hear from him all the time. We went over some of it, and boy, -- he's the guy that really did The One O'Clock Jump. The score was there, he brought the music, played it off this -- and the other way the other parts got added in was, like, it didn't have nothing to do with the trombones because everybody was hitting the same way and always could come up with something. A guy would say, now, let's see you put something in this, genius. And I'd just start that -- me and Dan, see. Buster made the statement that Dan did it, but it was me and Dan. Of course, it doesn't make any difference,
but that's how he did it. Then they started calling me Circus Boy. There's old Circus.
Well, why was it then that -- you know, with this talent, why was it that he seemed as though he always wanted to stay at home?
Buster?
Yeah. I mean, he never --
Well, he don't like to travel.
Oh.
He won't fly at all.
Oh.
He ain't particular about busses and things, boats. He rides a bus or a train, but he wouldn't fly even to Kansas City. He's a superstitious type of fellow.
What?
Superstitious type of fellow, and he ain't got a hair on his head, not a grey hair in his head, right today.
He's your age, isn't he?
No. No, not that type of aging. He don't look old, because I came --
But, I mean, he's as old as you, isn't he?
Yeah, he's a little older than me, about 72. And I came in and I sat right beside him in -- right
down in a seat beside him, and I got up and said, when is Buster Smith coming in? Everybody started laughing, place was packed. Joe Thomas was there --
Oh, this is when you did this Kansas City --
He said, you ain't going to speak to your buddy? You just got up beside him. I didn't (inaudible), so we stayed together. But the guy is terrific.
He still plays?

Yeah, he plays a -- he doesn't -- I was thinking about bringing him here and letting him work out back. He plays bass, he played piano in a concert. Did one number for me, and after that, (inaudible) not playing no more. He say, go ahead, I will find any number for anybody. So he played for Bud and all the other thing. (Inaudible) he was at the piano and he just played anything.
Did you hear that record he made about five or six years ago?
Well, he made something with me, I know. Thing like Morton Swing and that stuff.
When did he make them? Oh, you mean, that was for Decca.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, but, now, I guess, five -- maybe it's ten years ago, he made an album, and he sounds good, but
as I remember, the band with wasn't too good.
Yeah, maybe so.
I think it was made in Dallas.
Well, he got disgusted with the alto, because --
Oh, he did?

Yeah. I was with him with he was teaching Charlie, Charlie Parker Casey, show him how to hold it. Put his hand here and there and blow this, and Charles wasn't reading. And I was teaching Christian at the same time, so that's why -- we made a script like that in the movie, he and I sat down and talked, and he told me, he say, you remember such-and-such a place when Charlie came by, he took the guitar off the wall and he played the piano?

And we both -- Charlie's tone was so bad, that Buster said -- discussed him, said, I don't want to play sax no more. And so Charlie was trying to play like Buster, all the time, but he didn't get what Buster played, so he come out with something of his own which made history for him. So that's the way that happened.
Well, now, whose tone was --
(End of Side One.)
Well, now, we were talking about Buster Smith. Oh, you were saying that he didn't like Charlie Parker's tone.
No, because he wanted Charlie to have another tone.
But he couldn't.
(Unintelligible.)
(Recording interrupted.)
I left the mike there and it picked up all that tone. Now, Buster Smith didn't like Charlie Parker's --
He was teaching him, he wanted to get a better tone.
Yeah.
Wanted Charlie to get a better tone.
But he couldn't get it?

Charlie didn't get into it and that sort of worried Buster, because the guys was cranky about tones in those days. So -- but, Charlie was trying to play like Buster, all his life, and he couldn't get Buster, so he materialized something that was of his own which created history, something for himself.
Yeah, but didn't you say that it was never a good tone for a section?
No, no, no.
Now, why is that not a good section tone?
Because you've got to play the same weight of vibrato. See, like, the white bands, the musician
plays one or two tones, the vibrato tone and the straight tone.
Right.

And that's why any white musician can sit down and play in Glenn Miller's band or someplace else. But the black musicians can get eight or ten different tones on his horn, so when he gets in a band, that's why it's hard for him to fit.
Well, now, the different tones, this had nothing to do with the vibrato, really.
Yeah, maybe, maybe not. Sometimes it's too much vibrato or not enough. It works for solo work, but sometimes it won't -- the other guys can't get it.
Well, that's the point. There's a problem blending when you've got different --
Got other things, got other the team with you, you've got to stay in line.
Yeah, yeah.
So Buster didn't like it because Charlie's tone as always bad.
But, now, you're saying --
But it was a tone the public went for.
Well, you say it was bad, but it was bad in relation to what?
To blend with the other saxes.
I see, not as compared, we'll say, with Johnny Hodges or Willie Smith or Benny Carter.
No.
I suppose it was bad in comparison with them.
Oh, yeah, it was -- because -- yeah, no, it wasn't --
But, I mean, when you come down to it, I mean, there was -- it was a good reason for people disliking Lester's tone, because, I mean, Cohn and Hawkins had sort of shown what the instrument could do.
Big headed fat tone.
I mean, which was great. And then he comes -- this sort of little whispery sound, more like an alto, almost.
Yeah, upon his horn.
But -- so you could very well say that that was a bad tone, too.
It was, yeah.
At the same time, he had enough -- his ideas were such that people accepted tone and all.
And then his style of playing fit that -- he was doing it, so it was just his solo individual deal.
Yeah, yeah.
But I'll say this, I found a way to use
it with the section.
Oh.
Yeah, when I used him up as a C melody part, which we call the alto part, I've never let him play the root of a chord.
I see.

Always kept him way up in the sixes and hard notes, laying right next to that second alto. If you ever move away from that, the weight will go away from the section, because he didn't have a big heavy tone. Keep him up in there, and that's how that section sounded different. When he came out, they put in two regular tenors, Basie's section started sounding like Fletch Henderson or somebody else's section. Where the tone was concerned.
Right, yeah, because when you get -- yeah, when you get people later, like Buddy Tate and Don Bias, you've got a different thing going.
Got a different thing going.
Yeah.
Well, what we were talking about there, when we got into Buster Smith, was about you joining the Blue Devils.
Yeah.
Now, tell us something about the Blue Devils.
Well, --
Who was the leader then?
Walter Page was the leader.
He was the leader. Was he the leader all along?

I learned that someone else must have been the leader, but he is the one that got me, see. And Buster. And that band, that's the way they played. They didn't have too big a band. Walter Page was playing bass on his baritone sax, playing bass on his baritone sax.
Why was he doing that?
Well, he played bass, too, but that's just something a lot of them used to do, because a bass sax can play bass on there, just like a bass horn, too.
Well, I mean, somebody once told me --
He didn't have a string bass.
Well, that was also because it was easier to carry the saxophone around than the string bass when you were just traveling in cars and --
Might have been. Might have, yeah, because we didn't have room for that bass.
That's what I mean.
And he started playing bass on that, and boy, he could pump it. And --
Bass on the baritone?
Yeah. And so when he come to play in Benny Morton's band, I wanted a little of that.
Now, when he -- no, he didn't play as a saxophone section. He played --
Bass.
He played bass -- yeah, I got you.
No, he didn't play with the saxophones. He'd get that baritone, he played bass.
But he just sort of played notes, sort of staccato.
Just like the bass player.
Yeah, yeah.
Boom boom-boom-boom, boom boom-boom-boom, see. And --
Well, just -- I don't want to appear too ignorant, here, but the effect, would that be more like the tuba than the string bass on a -- or would it --
It'd be more like string bass. In between. It's like the tuba, but it's in between.
He could move on those.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So I wrote a little of that with different bands at times, you know. That's why we used to -- a lot of arrangers, way back, when they had a baritone,
like Lunafords band, a lot of times I wrote the bass -- baritone with the bass. You didn't even know it, saxes going nowhere and the baritone, he's going with the bass.
Yeah, I think you can hear that on some of the records.
Yeah. We didn't make it distinctive, just solely bass all the time. But I'd move into that bass with the baritone, sustain it, yeah.
Would it give it a sort of -- now, what --
Give it a heavy reed tone in that bass section.
Yeah, but it takes away from the sax section.
No, it didn't bother the sax section.
This was when they had five saxes, or four?
Four.
And you put the baritone playing with the bass?
Sometimes, in some spots, like Running A Temperature. If you listen close, the baritone is going out in a direction away from the other saxes all together. In Running A Temperature.
Well, I can tell where that would sound
The baritone carries.
Yeah.
It carries.
Carried more than the bass?
Yeah, more than the other saxes.
Well, you felt the bass, but you didn't hear it very often.
Yeah, baritone carries heavy.
Yeah.
Carries a lot of volume.
That was really a good idea, because --
I know -- quite a few bands out West now that are doing it. Not all the time, but they'll find a place where they play bass with that baritone, staccato bass, you know.

Yeah, because -- also, you know, even when they started to get electric amplification, they -- you couldn't -- it wasn't that good, was it, in' the beginning. Very often, if you were in a crowded place, like the Renaissance or something, you couldn't hear the bass.
No, you couldn't hear the bass.
You really couldn't. Too many bodies in the way.
Then they got so they'd put a mike pretty
close to it, and that was too broad. The mike would make it bounce too big.
Yeah.
So the bass wasn't heard too well.
Sort of a boomy sound.

Yeah. I think that had a lot to do with the rock taking over, too, from the jazz. Because the rock come in there with that electric bass, and you could hear that bass. And I always figured that the rhythm sections was too little for a 16, 17-piece band. Always felt that.
Well, I suppose that partly was the reason they started to fool around with the conga drums.
Yeah, they did.
That always seemed a bad idea to me.
Yeah.
I mean, that made a muddly sort of --
Too much muddling and too much execution and all that sound, yeah.
Well, who else was in the Blue Devils when you joined them?
Let me see, it was Lips Page, Walter Page, Buster Smith, Dan Miner, -- who they never mention, he came from there into Benny Morton's band, trombone player.
Yeah.
And I can't think who else was there at
the present time. I don't know if Bert Johnson was there at that time or not. But I think Booker Pitten was over there.
Booker Pittman was there?
I think so. But I know I named the ones that I remember was there. Just like I say, Page and Buster Smith, Lips Page, Dan Miner, and I've forgotten now, we had some boy singing there, too.
And the drummer was Alvin Burrows?
Yeah.
And I know that the piano player one time was somebody called Lovingsgood or something. But on the record -- was Jimmy Rushing singing with the band then when you were there?
Yeah.
He was?
I forgot about Rushing. I believe -- yeah.
Well, so that was really a very good little band.
Yeah.
In those time, wasn't it?
Yeah.
And you were playing trombone?
Yeah, I played trombone.
So there were two trombones.
Yeah. Dan Miner -- and I don't know if I played guitar. I didn't stay there too long. The money was light.
Well, they weren't doing too well?
No, they didn't do too good, so we broke up. I say, I'm going -- I went up there and got with Benny Morton. Big pay, say, let's all the rest of us go. That's how they started drifting away.
Well, how did they -- so a whole lot of people from that band went into Benny Morton's band. Well, who did they replace then? I mean, --
The Blue Devils?
Yeah.
I think they broke up, didn't they?
The Blue Devils broke up, but then when you all went into Basie's band, did his band get bigger, or did he --
No, that was the Benny Morton band. And Verlon Page, who played the tuba, Big Page come in his place, you understand?
Yeah.
And the band got bigger.
Yeah.
Because they only had two trumpets and a trombone, Ed Lewis and Booker Washington and Thman Hayes. But
when I came in, then that made four of us. Then when Lips came in, that made five. Then they added another trumpet, it made six.
Yeah.
And the same with the reed section.
The reed section went from three up to four.
Well, I mean, that was happening really with all the bands at that time, wasn't it?
Yeah, switching around and eventually the banjo player went out.
Yeah.
And I played guitar, and they got old Freddie Green right away, you know.
Tell me something about Walter Page. What do you remember of him in those days? I mean, he was a good musician, wasn't he?

One thing about Page, he could master tone or filler. He could be heard without amplifying. Big hands and arms, I don't know how he hit those notes, but when he would hit a note, the vibration would vibrate in any room, and the stage would sway.
That was (inaudible) with strength?
Strength, I believe.
Then he was a strong guy, wasn't he?
Yeah, big, strong guy. Then he would
hug the bass like this, and he said his body and things had a lot to do with the tone of the bass, too.
Yeah.

And the way he'd hit the note, you know. Like, a lot of guys pick it like this? He used to hit those notes. Big, like that. That was the style then, and Mose Allen wasn't a great bass player, but he used that style and -- he didn't play many notes, though.
Well, he sort of -- he slapped more.

Yeah, he didn't have much tone, but Stanfield and Hawkins kind of had a big tone like that. But at the present time, Gene Ramey is the guy with that big solid tone. Not naming other musicians, but he's a little bigger than some of the greater guys in those days.
Yeah.
They toned him down. Because I think using that amplifier -- leaning on the amplifier a lot, some of the guys.
But it always seemed to me, too, that Gene Ramey sort of somehow held the notes a little longer than most of them.
Could be, too.
A sort of longer sound on them.
Yeah, he'd hit those notes, and -- boom, because in Kansas City, let's see, Buster Smith was playing
the piano and Gene Ramey was playing the bass and Joe Jones on the drums and I'm playing guitar.
This is when you did this --
People like Susan Strasberger, they thought that was the greatest thing they ever heard. Oh, you should have heard that rhythm section.
Yeah.
With Buster Smith and Joe Jones and Gene Ramey.
Buster can play enough piano to impress you, can't he?
Yeah. Yeah, he fit right in there. Strong, with a bassist style, but he was so heavy with it.
Yeah.

I mean, it's so -- the way his voice -- in that rhythm section, it was something, because I was doing all the solo work at the time, _______ the trombone. So we just cut out all the band. I did quite a few things, just the three of us.
Well, do you think he'd come up to New York for awhile?
Yeah, sure he will. I want to get him to up and play. I'm going to get in touch with him right away.
Well, the only thing is, you have -- I
mean, you've only got, like, sort of two or three days a week, haven't you?
Yeah, two and three. I can as many days as I want to, other places.
Yeah.

Oh, man, I've just been so busy, my kids come in and try to buy this place and all that, and try to get the property I got over here and all those things, and Battles' dying now, and fooling around with all of that. The girl is right on top of me. She can't -- they don't do nothing without me. They don't know nothing.
No.
I found the land for them. Everybody, and everybody else.
Is Buster Smith married?
Yeah, he's -- yeah, he has children, but they all left home and he's in the house by hisself.
But his wife is still living?
He and his wife. So he don't do nothing but go fishing and --
So, maybe he --

Lately, a couple of times, we started (inaudible) coming out. You don't need but one night a week, one or two nights, as long as he got somewhere to stay. He don't care whether -- if he got somewhere to stay, he'll just
come. Won't cost him nothing to live. He could live in the city, out in my place out here. Or either out there at the hotel. It won't cost him nothing. And he can play, too.
Well, I don't --
Put him on two nights.
It'd be wonderful if you could do it.

I will, because that -- see, I'm writing a score now for about eight pieces.
