How long were you with them?
I must have been with Willy about six months, maybe, not that -- yeah, that's about all. I went to Jimmy Lunsford's band, I think.
But Willy's band was pretty good at that time.
Good band.
Was Benny Carter in it when you --
Benny Carter was playing the alto. Lorenzo Pack and Johnny Russell and Cozy Cole.
Yeah.
In the rhythm section and Teddy Wilson
playing piano.
Yeah, it was a good band.
Yeah. I can name a few other guys.
was there on trombone, he wasn't too good. But, yeah, I played --
Now, the arrangement -- which was the arrangement you said you remember?
The Chimes in the Chapel.
Chimes in the Chapel, yeah.
It don't look like they changed the title, there, Chimes at the Meeting. Maybe they took the word out, Chapel.
Chimes in the Meeting, oh, they changed it.
Yeah, I think they did.
Yeah.

I think I heard something like that, the record -- they didn't want to use the chapel. But he used to sing it Chimes in the Chapel. It had chimes in it, too, you know, like, ringing bells and stuff like that.
Was Ben Webster in that when you were there?
No, it was Lorenzo Pack, --
Johnny Russell.
And Johnny Russell and Benny Carter,
that's all. And the trumpet section was Battles and --
Bobby Cheek?
Clark.
Richard Clark.
Richard Clark. Battles, Clark, and I forgot who else --
Well, the guy they've got down in the book is Bobby Cheek, and later they had Jack Butler and Taft Jordan.
They must have come in after I was there.
Ah ha.
Yeah, I think they came in afterwards. Or either before. It must have been afterwards.
Well, when you were playing with them, did he do as he does on the records, sing on nearly all of them?
Yeah, he was doing a lot of singing.
Why was he doing that? Did he think he could -- he thought he could make it as a singer?
Yeah. Yeah, he was (inaudible).
Well, I suppose that was the time when Cab Calloway was making everything.
Yeah, yeah. And he figured, he wasn't a musician, so he was going to try to do something, direct
and sing, so he was singing most everything.
Well, he was a pretty popular guy in Harlem at that time, wasn't it?
He had a gold pistol and everything.
What?
He was the mayor of the town, he had a gold pistol.
A gold pistol?
Yeah, Willy Bryant had a gold pistol.
What did he have that for?
He was the mayor of Harlem.
Oh.
Music mayor. Yeah.
Well, he was quite a ladies' man, too, wasn't he?
Yeah.
Well, now, when you leave him to go to Lunceford, how did that come about?
Well, you see, after the union was bothering me so much, I didn't like to be antagonized, waiting around like that, and then I just -- I went to a band where I could play.
Well, now, when you came into a city like New York, how long did you have to sit around before you could --
Six months.
Well, how did they think you lived?
Let's see, now, how did you do that? You'd have to sweat it out some kind of way.
Well, when did they change that?
Quite a while -- quite a few years back.
What do you have to do now?
You have to put in an application, and you sign up and go on the application as a traveling member.
Yeah.

And if you was in the city, you had to go out and play dates out until you became a member, but you had to let them know when you went out and came back. You'd live in the city and go get your gig somewhere else.
So you could -- but once you'd done that, you could be, like, a member of a Chicago local and New York, could you?

Yeah, you could stay with both locals if you wanted to, but you had two dues to pay. I did it, I belonged to four unions at one time for a long time. To 627 in Kansas City, 710, Washington, D. C., I was on the board of directors there, at the same time I belonged to New York City and I belonged to the union in Connecticut.
Well, what is the position today? I'm never quite clear about that. I mean, if you're a member --
I don't think you put transfers in there.
If you're a member of the union, you're a member of the union.
Yeah, you just pay white dues. Like up here where we are, I pay $60 a month.
But that's the local.
Yeah.
I got you.
Yeah, setting half of the scale, I think.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So then, you go with -- how did Lunceford --
Get me?
Yeah.

Well, see, Paul Weber is a trumpet player, Eddie Thompson is a trumpet player. After we broke up the five clique, we had the three clique, In Kansas City, like, you call up and say, Eddie Thompson, I'd like to play for my band tonight. Say, I can't play, I got all trumpet or all trombone. Can you use him?
Well, who was left in the three clique?
In the three?
You said there was a --
Eddie Tomkins, myself and Paul Webster.
Oh, that was the three.
Yeah, we lost the other trumpet, and we lost Keg on the trombone.
Yeah, they left town.
Yeah, he went on with Cab or somewhere.
Yeah.
And he plays a trio.
So now the three of you are in the Lunceford band.
Yeah, well, they was trying to get me to come down to Lunceford all the time. So eventually, Lunceford came to New York.
Yeah.

And they said, we'll get him. And I was with Willy Pratt and I wasn't playing regular, because every time a __________ would come out, I'd have to sit back, I couldn't go on the stand. And I went over to Lunceford band, first time I heard it, they'd been trying to get me for about four years. Because when school would start, Paul Webster and Eddie would come back, because Paul was taking a mortician and Eddie was being a doctor. Eddie __________ went up to seven years --
Did what?
He was in his seventh year when he
left, of being a doctor. And that was in the University of Iowa.
Oh, yeah?

Yeah, but he got in so much trouble all the time. They suspended him the last year because he went -- we would always go down to the school at night and get into the laboratory and get whisky and stuff for the band.

And he got (inaudible) all drunk and he knocked over something and started a fire. He got burned, got burned in there, and they had to get him out. And they put him out of the school because he'd been doing it all along. But they'd go to school, and as soon as school was out, they'd tear to Buffalo and join Lunceford's band. They'd say, Lunceford, we got a trombone man with us.
And, quite naturally, when they played anything, we had our own routines.
Yeah.

We could get in the band and the brass would take over a couple of choruses. And that's how I got in Lunceford's band. He was playing the Parlor, and I went down and heard the band, I thought the band was fantastic, it was a show band.
Yeah.
So I said, I think I'll come in, because Lunceford was paying $35 a week or something like
that.
Now, how did that sort of Lunceford style -- I mean, the style of the thing, how did that hit you? Did you like it?
Well, the music wasn't all that great, but they just had a variety of novelty.
Yeah.
Dancing, they had a dancing chorus. Six of the guys come out and do the dance.
Now, I never did --
(Unintelligible) they'd come out and do a whole routine with the chorus boys. By the time they'd get back, there's the glee club and they had a trio.
Oh, yeah, I mean --

So then, I was the guy that could really voice that harmony for myself, because they didn't have but five horns and they weren't writing for six horns. So that's why the repertoire was short on my part, when the trombone went in my place.

Lunceford told me we have to teach him. Three weeks and you can lead the band, I didn't know you could lead anyway. Because there wasn't that much music. So they just started -- let him do a lot of solo work and then we don't have to worry too much, because you see, the guys wasn't writing good harmony in those days, not six-part. So I had to kind of get
in there and work Wilcox and Sy and all of them with that six-part harmony.
So that's how I got in Lunceford's band. And the reason I left Lunceford, because he never did get me no further than $60, $65 a week. And I joined Basie for $150.
$65 -- when did you join Lunceford?
It must have been '38. I stayed with him four years, didn't I?
Well, I was wondering, you got $65 then?
Well, I mean, that's --

He gave me $35 when I first started. But (unintelligible) when on and made $4,000 or $5,000 in one night. And so they had a corporation, and when he went to Larchmont from that air. He went on the air and then he said, there ain't no more corporation.
Oh, that was when the corporation --
It was all the cut rate, and the guys said, man, we ain't going to get cut and he said, we can't handle it no more. Ain't got it no more. (Unintelligible.)
That's when it started to break up then.

Yeah. Then, they played a date and John Hammond came out and saw me and I said, well, -- he said, Basie's short. I said, well, I promised to come back for a year. And Basie running short, he said, they only got
12 numbers and your arrangements in the Roseland, they need more stuff like that. And they ain't got nobody to write it. I said, well, I told you (unintelligible). I say, I'll come over.
So I gave Lunceford notice. And they gave me $75 for playing and $75 for arranging. I went into the big money.
That was a big step up.
(Unintelligible) Willy Smith, and--
Let's just talk a little more about Lunceford, though, now. What were the main things you arranged for him?
I made his Harlem Shout.
Yes.
That's that Harlem Shout album. And I made his Lunceford Special album. And I did numbers like Bird of Paradise.
That was the one -- that was Duke's tune.
Yeah.
That was the one you worked on with -- didn't you have to work with Eddie Wilcox on that?
With the piano?
Yeah.
Yeah, he could play. And I did a lot of horn work, Running a Temperature, and --
Oh, Boy?
Oh, Boy, and Hitting the Bottle and --
Avalon?

Avalon, and (inaudible). And I wrote one in there he called Oh, Eddie. These originals, because we made a lot of arrangements. Well, Running A Temperature and those wasn't arrangements, but a lot of those others --
(Inaudible) you did?
Yeah. And I can't think of all of the rest of them.
So all this time, the -- you and Sy Oliver were both sort of writing arrangements.
Yeah.
Well, that was a good idea, in a way, because there was a contrast, wasn't there?
Yeah, uh-huh.
You know, the styles were different.
Yeah. And then I did Swinging on a , the same thing Earl Hines did.
Oh, yes, yes.

I could name a lot of them. But I was taking up a lot of times, trying to help the guys voicing that six-part. They didn't have any knowledge in that. Then I wrote a lot of things where we used five saxes, too. But I used Dan Grisson on the sax.
Yeah.
See, and that was, like, Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me, and a few other things.
Yeah, so --
If you notice close, he's playing saxophone on that, the singer.
Well, I was going to ask you about that. I mean, now, you've had a lot of experience with different bands. How did you feel about that sax section?
With Lunceford?
Yeah.

It was a novelty section, and the powerhouse was Willy Smith. And so that made it different from other bands, because he was so strong. He played saxophone so loud that we never did write any in the background, at no time, with the reeds.
You think he played too strong?

Oh, yeah, he was as loud as the whole brass section. And whenever the reeds was playing a little harmonies, Smith would be on his horn and we didn't write him no part because he could never get it down. He'd be strong.
Really, then he was too strong.
Yeah, yeah. They liked him too strong where he really played, so he just (unintelligible). That was one of the secrets of the band.
And then, Crawford had a lot to do with that band.
Yeah.
Because he had his own style on the drum. That two-beat thing and all that helped Lunceford's band. I imagine that would work all right now, I guess. Two beats, like that.
Well, the way they did it, it wasn't corny, was it?
Well, Sy is doing in now, I think.
Oh, yes.
That's what the boys say.
And people like it. Yeah, because the rhythm section, apart from Crawford, wasn't that strong, was it?
No, because Mose was a very -- he wasn't a real -- you would say, a great bass player.
No.
He was just a two-beat man.
Yeah.

So I guess that helped. Because if we'd got some other guy that was strong in another style, it would have confused the thing. So he just wrote on top of Crawford. Crawford was the leader. Crawford played first drums in the band, and Mose played second fiddle.
Was Trummy there while you were there?
Trummy took my place.
Okay, so why did you leave that band?
Money.
Money spoke, did it?
Yeah, and the band travelled --
Well, they joined -- that's right, so they say you're going with Lunceford in '35, early '35 and joined Basie in '37.
About three years, right?
Yeah.
That's about right. And when I joined, the night I was supposed to join Lunceford, they booked the battle of music in Connecticut, something like that, -- no, a little further.
Bridgeport?
No, it must have been the other town, a little bigger than that. Stamford, I guess. What's that other town up there in Connecticut? Big, where they played a lot of dances.
The only place that I ever knew was the Ritz in Bridgeport.
No, it was another place, too, up there.
Oh, you don't mean this ________?
No, it was (inaudible). Bridgeport -- there's another town up there.
It wasn't Hartford.
Hartford.
Yeah.

That's the town. And so they had me up there a day ahead of the concert. You know how they do those gimmicks, because they interviewed me on a radio program that day. Said, we got the man here that was with Basie three years ago, been with Lunceford and he's going back to Basie, and he's going to tell you what he thinks about how this battle is going to come out. One of them old Mohammed Ali things.
So they had me on and they asked me --
Oh, this was the night you joined Lunceford.
Yeah, this was the day before the night. I was finishing with Basie that night and joining Lunceford the next night. So the bands played a battle of the music, battle of the bands.
Lunceford and Basie.
Yeah.
Yeah.

See, so that day they interviewed me about the difference in the bands. And they was trying to play up a big box office, so I made both bands the greatest bands in the world on each side, of this and that. And all

that and everything.

So that night, when Basie played his last tune, I think Lunceford -- no, Basie closed. And I had Basie's valet to come over and get my stuff and set it over on that side. So the promoters took advantage of it, because they had me on the air then, for about two hours on the program. Asked -- pumping questions about these two bands.

And you couldn't get anyplace. People tore the place up. They tore the place up.
Well, who won this battle?
Oh, --
Because Basie, today, if you talk to Basie, -- and I've often said to him, well, all right, now, what other bands really swung? And he'd always say Lunceford.
Lunceford wasn't too much of a swinging band.
It was a --
It was a novelty band.
But you had these tempos.
He had a beat like that.
Yeah.

But that beat, that's a good beat.

But that beat today, the guys play too much rhythm these days, now. You couldn't go all night like that. Sy can get away with it because he got a lot of other stuff with it.
Yeah.
He colors it, you know what I mean? And he's playing to a smoother place. He ain't playing all this old rough, heavy stuff.
But your things were mostly written sort of like Basie would, for four-four.
Yeah, I liked that.
Well, that was good for Lunceford to have as a contrast, wasn't it?
He had a style.
Yeah, yeah.
Sy would do a good job with it, but he ain't got a big enough band. He say he just can't afford (inaudible).

Well, one thing I'll say for that band Sy's got now is that at least it's regular work. I mean, there's guys up there that are now working up there about 40 weeks out of the year or 30 weeks out of the year. And I don't know, must be fairly good in that room, I should think, wouldn't it?
Yeah. But I do say this: Sy has got the biggest little band left, now. He's the only one that's got it.
Yeah.
And I think he's holding up well. In
order to stay there as long as he is and keep this thing going, he's got to have something on the ball.

Well, I'll tell you, it's just what you were saying, though, about -- you say that was a novelty band. Basie said that -- he said, oh, they get up there and get the thing going and swing all night long. Well, of course, it was a type of swing.
Yeah, yeah.
There was a difference. But, you see, I think it's one of those things that people who are dancing like. I've been up there with --
Well, they can understand that two-beat --

That's right. And, of course, Sy always has a fair amount of melody for them. Some of them are dancing to the melody as much as -- but, anyway, when you went to Basie, this wasn't such a big change to you, because you --
(Inaudible), didn't need any music.
No, but after all, you'd been with Moten and everything, hadn't you?
Yeah, and I'd been with Basie and I knew what he was playing and everything else. It wasn't nothing.
Right.
(Inaudible) overnight. And I had a

good memory. Lunceford went to Europe and he had -- Lunceford had some 300 numbers in his repertoire. And I never pulled my book out, never. And when I go to Basie and play and go back up to Lunceford, I still didn't have to pull it out. Which might not have been so good for me then, because I remembered a lot of things myself. But, boy, they didn't pull no book out for me in those bands.

Well, now, this is when -- let's see, Dickie Rouse says that you and Basie got together on a whole lot of things now, though, for the band, because the band was the band's personnel was changing a bit, wasn't it?
Yeah, well, I gave it a story -- we didn't get on anything -- well, Digger Wells went in my place.
Dickie took your place?

Yeah. They were playing the Shady Rest in Newark, big place, packed. They opened at 9:00, I got there about 9:30. When I got there I had put my uniform on, Dickie Wells come up with my book under his arm, and his on. I said, here's your new trombone player.
How long were you with Basie then?
Stayed a year.
Huh?
One year.
Oh, not more than that?
No.
Well, why did you leave Basie?
I left Basie because I had been with Lunceford. And Lunceford's band was so polished, society-type wise, --
Yeah.
And I thought Basie wasn't being business enough. Basie was always -- he always wanted a good time with me, he didn't want to do any writing.
Well, actually, the band -
And I said -- I just left that .
The band, though, was improving at this time, wasn't it?

Yeah. Well, I said I'll be here a year, and that's as long as I stayed. It seemed like it wasn't moving fast enough for you, you see. Because I was out to write and play, and Basie wanted a good time a lot. "This is your band, just like me, you ain't supposed to --" He'd go into one of those things, and, boy.

And we used to with Benny Moten and say, someday we're going to have our own band, and we're going to set in a car and ride. The bus would be in front of us, and "there's my Cadillac," and I'd say yeah, well, I ain't waiting for you tonight. And that's the way he thought. He say, you ain't supposed to be over here working, you're supposed
to be having a good time.
But he, now -- Basie at that point, he wanted to keep -- I take it he wanted to keep the arrangements sort of fairly simple, didn't he?
Yes.
I mean, he didn't want anything sort of ambitious.
No, he didn't care about way out stuff.
Yeah.

Because, like, if anybody brought arrangements around that was a little odd, he didn't want to play it. And the only way (inaudible) play it. And Buck was writing nice. And he wouldn't play Buck's arrangements. And a lot of time when he'd be getting ready to call the numbers, I would tell him to play these two numbers Buck did yesterday, and that's how they got playing. So Buck's numbers got played like that. And so I was the instigator.

But Basie's all right, but he always kept remembering what a hard time we had, and why should I work hard? I could hire somebody to write. And when I came back in the band, that's what he did. He said, now, Ed, you meet them in Albany, New York. I got the train and I went to Albany and I met the band.
And when I got there, I wrote Topsy on the train, on the way there. Sat down and just thought it, wrote it up

and got there, and they was already in rehearsal, out at the park. And I went out there and I had -- couldn't make no score because I didn't have time. I wanted to have something in rehearsal. And Harry Edison, those guys sat down and -- I made some score and they struck it off. And that's why they -- all embarrass Edgar so when they see him, because they wonder, how did he get on this sort of music?
I see that Parnassie -- we mentioned all the ones with Lunceford except Wham. He mentioned Wham was one of the Lunceford's.
Yeah, that was originally made for Benny Moten.
Originally?
Yeah.
Oh.

Well, here's the way it was. Taps Miller had the lyrics. He went to Basie, Basie wouldn't do them because they was all out of meter and he didn't have the meters, he couldn't fit the words with the music.
Yeah.

So I listened to it and Tap said, well, I need this band, Basie won't do it. I said, well, I'll fix it so he'll do it. And I made it, and so Glenn Miller was recording, and Glenn gave me two numbers to make up for ____. And I made up -- like, Wham, that went on -- by

me straightening it out for Basie, I said, let me let Glenn play it. And Glenn wouldn't play arrangements with pencil, so I carried in the pencil copy, go over this, let's see. And I say, take it up and I'll have it -- he said, you're not taking this noplace. He say, Glenn took this arrangement, no, you're not getting this. We're going to play this (unintelligible). Say, that's good for ______. I say, yeah, yeah, so that's how they got that.

So and then Taps -- I told Taps, now, anything Glenn does, I gives him 50 percent of the original because his name was big. So it's better to let him have 50 percent of your song, Stanley, than to have it laying up to today and it wouldn't be known.
Yeah, that's true.
But he didn't want his name on it. He said, no, no, because he'd been around too long and they'd pick up on the style.
Yeah.
So he said, I'll do the numbers, just give me 50 percent of the writership.

Well, I suppose when you see, like, Benny Goodman's name on Stomping at the Savoy or Harry James has got his name on Duke's I'm Beginning to See the Light, I suppose in a way it is worthwhile giving a share of a song away.
If he didn't do it, it might never have been done.
That's right. But the only thing is, when you do that, you give away 50 percent of a song.
That's right.
And then it's a hell of a big hit, you're apt to feel a little bit sorry that you did it.
Yeah.
But you have to be --
But you sure good that you got on the map.
Well, that's right.
You got on the chart.
But I guess not everybody can look at it that way.

You know why? Because they don't go back and write another one. As soon as you do that, then you go back and you write something else. If you can write another one, you don't worry too much. But the guy that can't write -- that'll never get nothing else, he's the one that's crazy.
Well, I know somebody was saying that -- you've heard those stories about Fats Waller selling songs (unintelligible) or something like that.
Yeah, yeah.

Well, I think that same thing happened with some of Johnny Hodges' things. You see, Duke would give him -- say, well, I'll give you a couple hundred dollars, and then Duke turns it into a big hit, and Johnny is sore. But --
So was (unintelligible) and all those guys.

Well, some of them had their names as top composers. When they sold them outright, then it was made a big hit, I mean, there was some of Duke's songs that you know those ideas came from Johnny Hodges. I mean, it sounds, (unintelligible) My Heart, I mean, that sounds exactly like Johnny, doesn't it?
Yeah.
But you've really got to be either philosophical or honest about something like that.
Yeah, but to be successful as a band-leader, I think you need the cooperation of talent from the men in your band, just like they do, you understand?
Yeah.

But if the name's on it with you, it's good and you pay them. But a lot of guys -- because the leader's name has to carry plenty. Just Johnny Hodges it wouldn't go as well as Duke Ellington and Johnny Hodges.
That's right, that's right.
(Unintelligible.)
That's right. So when you said this, about 50 percent, do you -- you didn't consider you were being taken advantage of at all.
Only thing I considered was, it's like pulling a hen's tooth to get a number recorded.
Like what?
Like pulling a hen's teeth.
Yeah.
To get a number recorded. If he didn't have a big man, he'd be laying on the shelf for 50 years.
That's right.
You had to get a -- guys are big, the guys that do that, get a guy to take some of it. And (unintelligible) made a dollar on that, he'd of never been in business.

The only thing that always seems to me is, we'll say Glenn Miller takes your tune and plays it on the air, records it, et cetera. That's fine. So then the thing becomes a hit. But, now, when we'll say Erskine Hawkins or Jimmy Lunceford or Tommy Dorsey start to play it, as well, because now it's a hit, Glenn Miller still got 50 percent of what they make.
Yeah, but I think -- you got to look at it another way, too. I look at it the other way. You lose a lot of money, but he's the man who started it for you.
Yes.

See? And now you can do it a little different, but those days you couldn't get past those managers. I wouldn't care what you had. If you didn't give up some of it, it wasn't going to get through noway.
No, well, I guess in a sense, too, it was rather -- in those days for a black writer to get through than it is now.
Yeah, and I'll tell you another thing. It was even hard for some of those little white ones to get through.
No, but there was a little bit of extra prejudice or whatever.
Yeah, yeah. So I'll say this: The only thing different was, --
Go on.
By Glenn Miller not putting his name on it left the credit to me.
Yeah, yeah.
And the credit comes to ASCAP, too.
Ah, I see. Yeah, well that was really pretty smart.
But the managers all wanted his name on it. But he insisted he wanted his name on nothing I did, because he said that style will cut through later years and

the critics will know it's his style and I want mine on the cover. But, Stanley, I just want to say one thing. The night, the tribute to John Hammond with Benny Goodman and George Benson and Benny Carter and all those on the air, --
Yeah.

Why was it that John went right to the mike and forgot that I named that tune after him when he was sitting in the audience? When we was rehearsing John's idea? And they asked him, how did it get its title? He said, well, it was a little thing that they just called John's Idea, for some reason. He never did say why. He never did say it was my tune. And the reason I brought it up, because four or five guys called me up about it. Couple of white guys called me, called me the next day, why didn't he say nothing about -- give you credit for that song?
John's Idea was your number?

Yeah, that was my number, yeah. And he happened to be sitting in the audience and I never could put a title on the thing, and I was rehearsing it. And I had a little idea for riffs in it, he was going -- and I said, Basie, let's name this John's Idea.
So I said, well, maybe he forgot it or something. But they said, well, they asked him how did it get its title. I said, well, maybe he forgot it.
He --
It was on the music there, right on the music.
He may have forgotten it.
I think he forgot it.
There would be -- well, I don't know, you can't -- John's Idea arrangement is Jimmy Mundy.
No, that's my number, and it's paying off pretty good now, too.
That's -- Basie's record was your arrangement.
Yeah. Maybe they made a mistake then.
Huh.
(Recording interrupted.)

Well, before we leave Basie, Eddie, I'd like -- you know, it's often been said that the Kansas City style was notable for its use of riffs. But as we both know, the (unintelligible) like Fletcher were using riffs before Basie came East, et cetera, et cetera.

Well, what would you say were the sort of most distinctive things about Kansas City jazz?

Well, the difference in the Kansas City riff and riffs other places out through the world was, the Kansas City riff always carried a melody that you could write a song from. All those riffs can be a song, like Lester Young with '77. That was a riff, but it made a melody. And some Symphony Sid
of the riffs that I heard up East, they didn't make good melodies.
No, they were just sort of like punctuations.

Yeah, I don't know what you'd call it, but the Kansas City riff, you could always write a song from it, like many of the riffs. Moten Swing, that was a riff, just made up for an ensemble to go along with Driving Me Crazy. Then we made a melody out of it.
Yeah.
And that's one of the numbers.
Well, that's a very good point. What else would you say about Kansas City jazz that was peculiar to it? I mean, rhythmically. Did they have a different conception of tempos or --

Well, they generally style a tempo that seemed to fit the public, not too fast and not too slow. Now, that was one of the secrets about the band when Basie got it. Basie's a genius in setting the tempo that'll charm a person, and that's true.

And that's one thing he had, was -- would let a band play that. And Jo Jones was responsible for a lot of that, too. Many bands made One O'Clock Jump, but I've never heard a band with the exact tempo that the Benny Moten band recorded. With Jo Jones -- was generally responsible for that
also. And -- but Basie would go along with it as leader, and he'd learn those tempos. I think he learned from Jo Jones, too.
Yeah.
But Jo was a master in that, setting those tempos.
Yeah. Well, Moten Swing itself is a good example of a tempo, isn't it? I mean, the original tempo they took that --
Yeah. But the other bands they play today, they don't ever get the right tempo.
No.
No, they don't, honestly. I play with a lot of them and they don't hit that groove that way.
But how do you think that ties up with the fact that in those days you were playing for dances and now they're sitting up on the concert stage, most of the time?

Well, today, that's why they do a lot of presentation concerts, where you're not dancing, so you can get away with faster tempos. But where you had to dance, there was the groove thing. In other words, you still can play those things, and Moten Swing could capture an audience just by sitting and listening just like they did in the theatre.
So you can't get away from the tempo. It hits the

human -- when it hits one human, it generally hits thousands, just exactly the right tempo, like Tequilla did. If it had been a little faster, it would have been different. That's one thing I express. The tempos mean everything. If you can get the tempo exactly what the public want, you can get the hit.

And Harlan Leonard did I Don't Want To Set The World On Fire, but he did it up in a speed tempo and that's why he didn't get over with that particular song. The same song would have caught right with the public. But when Tommy Tucker --
Was that -- whose song was that?
Myself and Benny Benjamin, we was writing together at that time.
Oh, that's right, yeah. Well, that must have been one of your biggest.
Yeah, it is one of the biggest, yeah.
Who made the hit on that?
Tommy Tucker got number one hit on it, just on the records. Then others followed up.

Well, there's one other thing about Kansas City I was going to say. What about -- I mean, Jay McShan, he has -- now, he has a sort of a pretty unique feeling, too, I always think. I always think he's very much underrated. He's -- it isn't quite like Basie's, but he does have a feeling for swing, doesn't he?
Yes, sir, he has that Western idea of getting that tempo down right.
Yeah.
And not of overexecuting. And the riffs he sets are still riffs that you can write songs from.
Yeah.
But they got a lot of them up East here that you can't write no songs from. I'll tell you, man.
Yeah.
Some of them are --

Yes. Do you think that -- it's one of my theories that the fact that he got Charlie Parker to New York in his band, that's all they ever have to say about Jay McShan; that Charlie Parker came to New York and he's --
Well, I think -- it's sleeping a little bit.
Hm?

It's sleeping on him a little bit. He's original man, and he offers a good feeling and everything, and he's playing his thing. He's a T-bone walker on the piano just like T-bone on the guitar, Christian was -- yeah, because Christian picked up -- he moved on into the Eastern style along with (unintelligible). And it wasn't nobody else playing it, so --
Well, --
It swung.
It's a sort of rhythmic gift, essentially, isn't it?
Yeah, that's right.
But, now, there was -- you know, when you set I Don't Want To Set The World On Fire, I was thinking of that other song that Fay Terro used to sing, Until The Real Thing Comes Along.
Until The Real Thing Comes Along.
Now, that's another example of a song that had to be sung at that tempo to make any sense.
That's right. And the way that got created, Fay Terro was a dancer.
Oh, was he?

And he had a dance team with a little fellow they called Van. And they got -- was getting a song together and they were dancers. And Van deceased. But they came to my house at 3:00 at night, and said, man, we got a song here, listen.

And I got up out of the bed and went down on the riverbank, and didn't have any manuscript paper. So I took some plain writing paper and made some lines and went down and sat on the riverbank and let them sing it. And I remember all the other words that they had, she had to correct. And they had lyrics in there, like I worked for you, I slaved by
fingers to the bone for you, I'll moan for you, I'll groan for you and all that. They eliminated that later.

But what happened, I wrote that out. So when I went back to Kansas City, about ten years ago, my wife's grandmother, my first wife, said, you left this thing up in the attic, that song I heard so much about. And she went up in the attic and had that original piece of paper I wrote that --
What did you do with that?
I fooled around and let it get away. She had a attic where she kept everything. She said, here's that thing, I heard that song was so big, look what you did, years ago.
Did you have your name on that?
No, I didn't write the song, they had --
Oh, I see, yeah.
I just wrote the music down for them on some writing paper, and that was still there for about 20 years up in the attic. And I said, I let that get away, that's history, and I couldn't find it.
So Fay Terro was singing in Andy's band.
Andy Capp, yeah.
So that's how it got in there.
Yeah.
I guess maybe Andy helped him out with it after he got there with the arrangements, or somebody
made arrangements on it.
Well, that was a pretty darn big hit for that time, wasn't it?
Yeah. A lot of things that come out, you don't know till you -- because that's --
Yeah. But, of course, they could sort of -- they couldn't play anything. They could cook it up in their heads --

That's all, they couldn't write the music or nothing. They hummed it to me and I wrote it down, right out there. But I had my old guitar with me, too, and we sat on the riverbank at 4:00 in the morning, that's how I wrote that down. Fay Terro and Van. And I gave him that lead sheet and he tore out with it. I don't know, maybe Mary Lou Williams might have made the arrangement on it. I don't know who made the arrangement. Andy would know, I guess.
Yeah, it was -- whatever it was, it was a very simple arrangement.
Yeah, but, see, I'm a guy never claimed nothing I didn't do. A lot of guys --
No, but it's just like --
Yeah, but they wanted me to go on the song with them.
You give away 50 percent -
Yeah, I could have went on the song
with them, but I didn't see why I should go on a song just for writing some notes down for some guys. But that's the racket today. But to me, that was dishonest, in those days.
Yeah, that was living up to your principles at that time. You wouldn't do that today, would you?

No, I wouldn't do that today. If I write anything today, more than likely I'll have to go on it because you're a part of it. You change the music around -- you know, I had to change a lot of the music, too.
Well, I was going to say, I'm sure that you don't know how many notes you put in there for it.
No, you don't. It was the only thing it was. It was pretty close to that melody, but they had enough there for three songs. Lyrics and things, I don't know.
Yes, well, that's a very good point about Kansas City.
There is something about that style of music that's distinctive. And I can't put it in words, though, I don't know what it was.
Well, the only thing -- there seemed to be a separate tradition, because, I mean, there was Joe Turner and Pete Johnson there, and there was that good old Julia Lee.
Yeah.
I always liked the way she treated a song. It wasn't great, but it was very communicative.
They had a terrific band, too. It didn't groove too much, but it was a swinging band like that. It didn't have much guts in it or something, I don't know. I don't know what that was.
Did you ever hear that other one, then, with Countess Johnson? She died very early, but she sang and played piano about then.
I think Jimmy Hamilton's wife was out there at the time.
Smith
Yeah, Vivian Green, I think, yeah.
No, but the one that you asked me about, I don't remember her.
Well, I've been told that she was very good, too. But there was another Johnson there, wasn't there? An Everett Johnson that played boogie-woogie and everything.
Yeah. And Juanita Bolo was around then. She's a jazz --
Who?
A girl named Juanita Bolo.
Oh, I don't know her.
She went up to -- she played with the band for the Traditional Jazz Club in Connecticut about four
years ago. She went up with Eddie Barefield and the band. She's from Kansas City.
Oh, yeah?
She worked with me a lot, and she plays the Kansas City style. She's gone back to Oklahoma. But a lot of them never did reach into the big time.
No. Not everybody could in those days. And how many years roughly were you in Kansas City?
'27,'28, and then I joined the Benny Moten band, I think, in '29. And I was in and out for about four years, I think, till '34, I believe, or '33.
Well, you had a good experience of it, anyway.

Yeah, yeah. It might have been -- let's see, maybe I was around Kansas City before '27. Yeah, I must have been moving awfully fast to play all those bands, because there was another band in there named Jack Allen. I didn't play with them, my brother was with that band. They had a gang of little bands there, since you bring it up.

Yeah, well, there was a lot of action there. And it seems as though it -- well, it had a lot to do with that -- what was it, the Pendergrast regime, things were corrupt and it's like when the Prohibition on in Harlem, there was more going on then than any other --
Well, see, our jobs -- Kansas City
never did close up.
Right.

Like the clubs close now with the bands, around 4:00. Kansas City bands come off the stage at 8:00 and 9:00 in the morning for people to go to work. And that's the way it was all night long, because they had liquor stores that stayed open 24 hours in Kansas City. When they did pass the law to close them up, one of the fellows stayed closed all day and at one minute after 12, he'd open up. And they carried him to court, and he said, well, I didn't open up today, I opened up this morning.
And so you'd stand there in line, right there on 18th and Vine, where you get the wine.
Yeah, well, it's all understandable that where there's a lot of night life, that's where the musicians congregate.

It's one thing about Kansas City that nobody never mentioned. After all the jobs was over, all the musicians would meet right on 18th and Vine, and the meeting place was right in the middle of the street.
Oh, yeah?
And Ben Webster used to get --
(End of Side One.)
So they all used to meet in the middle of the street.

Later, after -- that was the third job, because they all would leave one job around 2:00 or 3:00 or 4:00, and go to another job, you see. When I'd get off around 3:00 or 4:00 at the Cherry Blossom or any of those places, I'd go down to Piney Brown's or down there where Joe Turner was bartending. When I'd walk in, I'd have my guitar throwed across my neck.
You had what?
The guitar, I had it swinging on my back.
Oh, yeah.

Then I'd go there and I'd jump up on the stage there and sit up on the bar and get the guitar, and Joe Turner would wipe his hands, and he'd come there and he'd sing, see, and Joe Turner would sing and Jo Jones would have his snare drum, he'd come in -- no, with his sock cymbal, and it'd be about three of us. And that was another job. We used to work there until about 7:00 the next morning.

And he didn't have to pay us anything, because when I'd come out, money'd be sticking all up -- rolled up and stuck into the guitar, and put it in Joe Turner's pocket and that's where I first met him, and we used to play like that.
So Kansas City was some town, you know? And when they'd get on the street real late, well, that's when they'd get in the middle of the street. And Ben Webster, very often

he would get him some wine and drink it, and he would always like to do things like a kid. And he'd get in the middle of the street car tracks and drink and turn his back the way the street car was coming, and would stand there and wouldn't move for the street car, see.

And maybe three or four street cars would jam up and he wouldn't move because he would fight you. The guys wouldn't bother him. And they'd call the cops. At the time the cops were getting ready to come, Ben would run and they couldn't find him. They always had that -- they'd say, what's that? Oh, Ben Webster in the middle of the street car track.
He was always mischievous, was he?
So that was Kansas City.
Yeah. Well, now, after Basie, we have to go -- left 1938, scored regularly for Ida Ray Hutton, Glenn Miller, Jan Savitt, Artie Shaw.
Does all that follow right on from Basie?
Yeah. And when I went to Artie Shaw, first I made was Them There Eyes.
Was what?
Them There Eyes, for Billie Holliday.
Oh, yes.
We went together, I went right over with her. I stayed about three or four weeks. She did, and when she left there she went to Basie and I went to Basie,
and began to write. Then I stayed over there a while and --
Well, what sort of work do you do now? All kinds, I take it, not just instrumentals, but sort of song arrangements?
I haven't been doing any outside arranging. I just wrote up a lot of charts for myself.
No, I mean this period when you're with --
Basie?
No, after Basie, when you're arranging for Glenn Miller, Artie Shaw, Ina Ray, what did you do?
Well, I traveled with Ina for a year. I traveled with the band all over the country.
Oh, you did?
Yeah, I traveled with that band.
How good a band was that?

It got to be a very good band. But the musicians, you had to hand pick them. I had to send to London, England to get a first trumpet player, because there wasn't a woman here that could reach even a high C. But I didn't use many high C's, but they couldn't even reach a good F with volume, so they sent me a girl from out of England, from the Conservatory and she could reach that note, so that band was pretty rough.
Because --
Did she have the usual instrumentation?
We used four saxes, and -- five, let me say. Yeah, four trumpets, three trombones and five saxes. That's what we had.
Did Ina sing?
Yeah.
And conduct.
Yeah, and could sing. Her clarinet playing wasn't fast enough. They all quit playing when I started writing for the band. The leaders wouldn't play no more. They were afraid of the arrangements.
And you travelled with them, too. Did you rehearse them, I suppose?

Oh, yeah, I'd rehearse them. Most times I picked the openings, just like one of the managers with the Giants. He pick who he want to open, I'd pick songs according to the audience in the theaters and places, because Ina couldn't do that.
Well, how popular was that band then?

Very, very popular. They had a -- we went ten weeks coast to coast in Chicago, the Choice Hour. Bing Crosby had it on one station at 10:00 and she had it on the hour, that way. And that was her only competition. That was the Rose Bowl, ten weeks. And I went out there three or four weeks ahead of time, and -- maybe Earl might remember this. I went out there three or four weeks ahead of time to

to write the show, write music strictly for that broadcast. They had a big broadcast. And Earl was there, and he sent his car up and his chauffeur while he was gone, three or four weeks. And I had his car, whatever his car was. He probably forgot. And he'd say, use my car while you're gone.
Somebody run into it and hit it with a while I had it.
Well, what sort of a book did they play? I mean, was it --
I'll tell you just what they played. Now, they had a -- in Madison Square Garden, they had a big thing with all the bands, big bands, all of them, Basie, too.
Yeah.

And I said, give me a spot right in front of Basie. I'd fit the spots in, and they'd say, yeah, the girls get what they want. I had One O'Clock Jump written, note for note, and one of the girls, they had her solo down just like Basie was playing, that's what they did. And that made the novelty good, because when they come on and hear Basie, that just knocked the guys out to play just exactly what Basie was playing.
It was a gag, you know? And there was a band out in Chicago they called Dick Jergen. That was --
Oh, Dick Jergen, yeah, I've heard of him.

Aragon Ballroom, big band. So they wanted to have a battle of the bands with Ina's band when it come through. And I went through and I said, I'll fix it. So I wrote Ina's two or three arrangements and I said, give me one of yours, and I took Ina's arrangements and I made another part of each part. Said, now I want the reed section to set like this, a boy and a girl, a boy and a girl, big stage. I said, the boys can sit a little behind.

I said, now, the two drums we can't use, but we'll use -- let's use Dick Jurgens's drummer with the bass, and the girl -- no, wait, I let the girl play the bass drum and I let him play without the bass. And that's what they called a double band, and they hadn't had that before, see, Stanley. So you know they had a good band when I took one of his girls because they read what they see. They could read what they see, and I knew the arrangements.
Well, now, when you say they were very popular, was it because they were girls or was it because they were --
Well, they favored them because they was girls.
Yeah.
But in the end, they were playing more than they thought they were going to play. They played at the -- they come out of rehearsal with the second band. I went

and got a new band. And they come out with the second band, and they opened in the Paramount Theatre in Newark. And Lola Lane was on the program, MGM was there, Mitchell Lewis and I and when they closed that theatre, after opening over here for two days, then they said, well, they could open at the Paramount in New York.
So I didn't like that. I said, they must be favoring the girls. There ain't no bands can go open out of rehearsal with a new band and go to the Paramount in New York.
Right.

I say -- but they could play. But you still needed a reputation behind you. Basie hadn't even got any -- and we opened up in Rochester, in a preview, and Duke came up, had Duke to come up and a few other guys, to see what they thought about the band.

And some of the guys said, well, I don't like the girls, they're playing too much like boys, because they had them fanning hats, and they said, that don't look nice. And they wanted pretty girls like a melody, like this. Ina Hutton didn't like this, see, I want to swing like Basie, so the band got so they could swing. They had good musicians, of course, We had this Alice Wills on trombone, who travelled (inaudible). And she played 26 instruments perfectly. Played 26 different instruments. And she was a blond, looked good, and she played (inaudible) and they traveled around together.
Got a girl out of a conservatory out of Zanesville, Ohio, played a piano. They could really play, see. So you had to have (inaudible) band but you got to know your limitations.
Yeah. You didn't conduct on stage or anything.

No, if I did, it would be from the wings sometimes, getting out of something, and she (inaudible). Nobody could see me because they didn't know -- but sometimes I'd have to start a number off, or get it started. And she'd make an entrance.
But she was hard to handle, and -- everybody favored her, though, guys like the Marx Brothers and all those guys. She hung around with all them guys. It was a big time band.
Oh, yes, well, we'll come to the other one in a few minutes, but now, what about Glenn Miller and how much did you do for him?

Well, I did quite a bit for him, but I didn't do it -- like, my contract called for two arrangements a week. But when I went in with the St. Louis Blues, when I come back to rehearsal, I could always improve it. You had to have gimmicks then, and I rehearsed on that maybe four weeks. And that band was the greatest sight-reading band I ever seen in my life, because all of my arrangements was passed out at 10:00 at night, in the Casino, to a big crowd. And

whatever the tempo was, that's what went down. That was just to let them get acquainted with me. And I rehearsed it, but I'd proof with no mistakes, so you know a band has got to be awfully good. They're playing all their top stuff and then here comes an arrangement --
Yeah, sure.

And then I'd rehearse it. So the reason I didn't do too much for him was because we rehearsed so much on one number. And like I rehearsed In The Mood, I had to go down to Manny's and buy the derbies and the hats and things. And I'd come up with no -- I'd come up short with arrangements, but Glenn Miller told the manager, just give him a check when he comes, we'll get him out of arranging, I don't need but one. Forget about six or eight in these three weeks. Let him give me one out of these six weeks.
Well, --
In The Mood, Tuxedo Junction, St. Louis Blues, those are all hits right behind each other.
All the bands in those days varied their programs much more than they do today, didn't they?
He didn't care. He said, forget about the arrangements. If he gets me one out of this year, that's all we need. So he got them, too.
Well, it seems to me --
I stayed with him until he went overseas,
Stanley.
Hm?
I stayed with him till he went overseas.
Oh, you did?

Yeah, they offered me captain's rating. They wanted me to take three months training to protect myself, and here was a girl -- Mazie, wasn't it? Mazie, and in the field he was going to give me a captain's rating, and I didn't want to go. I didn't want to go overseas. I didn't want to travel overseas at all.

So we didn't let the band know it until they got ready to leave, and I came down, the first one I saw was Ina Hutton. Well, here's Eddie, he's -- oh, yeah, no, I would have been in there playing with him because I went everywhere he went when I was in that band, all the time I was with him. Went everywhere he went.
Well, there was -- but that was a -- that went on for how long with him?
I was there about a year and a half or something like that.
Oh, yeah.
And he told me two years. I said, Glenn, I think I can stay with you two years.
Is it then that you -- oh, it says was
musical director but formed own big band in June '41.

In 1940, I had a big band in the Oak Grove Casino. That's the one I'm going to give you a picture of. And I went from there to Glenn Miller. Now, I might have got another band after I left him, I don't remember.
It said --
Oh, I think I got the girls' band.
It said, formed own big band in June 1940, later that year was musical director for Bon Bon Tunnelle and his Buddies.
Yeah, that's what it was.
What sort of band was Bon Bon Tunnelle and his Buddies? Was he the guy that had been with Jan Savitt?
Yeah.
He was a singer.
Yeah. He didn't want the band in my name, so we put it in his name.
And then, --

We did a few shows. We went out and played (inaudible) quite a few theaters. And then Bon, he was married to a very wealthy girl, and she decided she didn't want him traveling. And he didn't show up at the Parlor, and they sued him and he quit and he paid off and paid his musicians off, and that's what broke that band up.. His wife
wouldn't let him go any further.
Now, then it said -- well, what about forming your own band in 1940? Do you remember that?
Yeah. That's the one I'm going to give you the picture of, on that location up there for 12 months.
Where did you work?
The Oak Grove Casino in Bridgeport, Connecticut. At Myrtle Beach.
Who did you have in it, anybody --

Yeah. My brass section was Freddy Webster, and Joe Keyes and Eddie Rowan. And Eddie left there and went with Louis Jordan. And my reed section was Buster Smith and this here Billy White, and Lem Johnson was in that band, and John Stovall came up there when he left the Metropol.

But, let me see, now, who took Don's place? I brought another white boy in, Tony Pasco's brother, he was a (unintelligible). And that's when Walter Winchell give me a writeup, to be the best band of the year.

And I left there and went to Glenn Miller. After we stayed up there, it was held over 16 more weeks. That's all in that paper there. And that's when I let the band go, because Mrs. Kramer come up there and somebody from the union. And he was telling me, this band -- they're not going to let you through, you sound like a white band and you're hurting the bands over here.

And they was playing Harry James and all those bands. It's a pleasure beach two miles from here, and it's paying them a lot of money and you -- let alone standing room, you couldn't get on the highway. (Unintelligible) coming from Connecticut, because Bon Bon was singing in the band, too, and that's the type of band I had with --
Who was singing?
Bon Bon was singing up there, too, with me.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah, he was (inaudible).
Who was booking you in those days then?
(Unintelligible.)
Ah, I was going to say, since you did well, if you'd got a booker they would have continued, wouldn't they?

Yeah, well, it hurt them so bad until they started to -- I was playing out on the pier, too. Came there one night and all the wires was cut. So I went to the D.A. and he made them give me some light on Sunday. And hook up to anything.

So I'll say this, the politicians was on me on one hand and the racketeers on the other. Politicians was trying to hold me there, but the racket men (inaudible). So I made a deal with the city by Pleasure Beach. If they wanted me to

the whites on a Sunday, see, because we lost so much money over here, with Harry James tonight and you over there. They said, you'd got to the whites. So I put up a sign I was going to the whites, and all the black musicians come down on me right away for segregating.
Yeah.

And I couldn't get out of that, and I went back and said you can't do that no more. I said, the whites -- and so, I said, well, I'll put up a sign, special party tonight, and I tried it that way and that wouldn't work. And those white kids was coming from New Haven and they wasn't going to play the (unintelligible). You can imagine what those guys -- the same (unintelligible). Ben Smith was in the band, then, too.
Yeah?
And he wrote that song, (unintelligible). And people could tell when you really had it, when you was really putting it down.
Well, what -- I mean, it says 1941, '43, toured as musical director for International Sweethearts of Rhythm.
That's when I went to the girls' band.
Well, you couldn't actually -- of course, this is getting into the wartime, isn't it, so things I suppose were getting a bit rough for bands, anyway.
Yeah, and I went to the girls' band.
Well, what made you do that?

Every time I would get a good band together, they'd draft the guys. And I just said, -- and so, the girls played the Apollo in Buchanan. I wasn't with them. They said, if you get over to a fellow named Eddie Durham, -- and when they got in touch with me again, that's when I went to Washington, D. C. and I went down and I rehearsed the band about ten days or so, and wrote St. Louis Blues.
And the war must have been on then, because we'd just come out of the Parlor Room, four weeks, and they didn't go ______.
Well, the war was on in Europe, but America wasn't in it.

I don't think so, no. I don't remember. But anyway, a number of the fellows came down and heard the band in rehearsal. Willard Wright came down and helped the band in a dance, and they came out to the house where I was rehearsing these girls. I took the little Chinese girl off alto and put her on baritone, and I got girls and I wrote two numbers and I rehearsed them like 10:00 in the morning till 10:00 at night. And then we'd give a dance, a trial. And I said, they're ready for the Apollo.
And sure enough, we played that dance and Willy Bryant came down there to M.C. the show (inaudible). Said,

man,that band will upset the place. So he came on to New York and I went to Nova Studio and made a demo at 8:00 at night. And Nola called it and went and called up Paul White, and said, I want to play something for you. Said, who do you think this is?

Well, I don't know, I don't know, it's great. He says, girls. He says, I don't believe it, but I'll be down there. Then he called up W.C. Handy and let him in, he say I'll be there with my trumpet to do an opening. But the musicians came back stage and they demanded to see this boys' band behind the curtains.

But, you see, it was the gimmicks and the tricks, and knowing how to make those girls in the tonation where they could play. So that's how I got over that band. And then I got some writeups. And so that's how I got involved in that.
Who were the girls -- what was the girl in that band who was a tenor player in that band that was very good.
Named Vy Burnside.
Hm?
Named Vy Burnside.
Ah, that's right, yeah.
She died.
Died?
About six, seven years ago. But there
was another girl I had in the other band, because I had to organize another band from the same man that owned the Sweethearts, to make money, and use the two bands.
