And a lot of fiddles were made out of cigar boxes today, I guess, and they put a seam in the middle of them and some good ones ain't got no seam. And then we'd go out -- and then he'd go out and kill him a rattlesnake. If he was 20 year s old, you'd have ten rattles -- no, if he was ten years old, he'd have 20 rattles. Then he'd kill a rattlesnake and he'd get the rattles and he'd bring them back and they'd dry those rattles for about four days. When they dry out, then they drop them down in the fiddle. When you hit the fiddle, boy,them rattles would sound -- that fiddle would sound like an amplifier.
(Laughter.)
It would what? Resound, you mean?
Yeah, if you put the rattles in it, the rattlesnake rattles. But you dry them out and put the rattles in it.
And do you get a vibrating sound or what kind of sound?
No, you just get a loud sound with that wood, you can hear little rattles.
You mean you fill it with the rattles?
Yeah, you put them inside the fiddle.
Do they about fill it up?
No, you would only put just about ten rattles in there, one set.
Is that right?

Because they come by sets and you just dry it out and you just drop them in there when they dry and then that gives the sound on that and I imagine it would be the same thing with acoustic guitar. So then -- and all the fiddle players would use it and I was a good shot, so I'd go out and get me about -- kill me about five or six rattlers, shoot them, then I cut the tail off and bring the rattle in and dry them out and you'd get 25 cents a rattle from downtown. They'd sell them to fiddle players.
: No kidding.
Sure, I used to (inaudible).
: How do you go out to kill a rattlesnake?
Oh, plenty of times, I went out.
: Well, how do you find them?
Turn over rocks. You know just about where they are.
: Isn't it dangerous?
Not if you're a good shot.
: You got to be quicker than the rattlesnake.
You don't get that close.
: You turn over a rock, you're pretty close.
Yeah, you turn over a rock and you jump back. You know they're under there and then they'll rattle at you, too, when you're walking.
: My gosh, you're wearing boots, I presume.
Wearing boots and look where you're going and maybe you can tell by when you throw something over there -- and they was infested out there in the West.
: Gosh.
But I (inaudible) rattlesnakes, I
went out and turn over a rock and you see at least ten down in there under the bed of a rock.
Well, wouldn't some of those get at you before you could shoot them?
Oh, they curl up to strike, but you ain't that close.
And if you kill one, the others will slither off or something?
They sure will. Everything runs from a bullet.
Is that right?
I don't understand that.
Is that right? You kill one and they all disappear?
If they can get away.
Is that right? They know that something else --
Yeah, soon as you shoot one, falls out, the rest of them know they no competition with that gun because you can back off where you want.
Well, I never -- well, listen --
Because one of them's running, I'd hit him in the head anyway (inaudible).
No kidding?
(Inaudible) get him.
Well, look, Eddie, before we -- I want to talk about that shooting, but before we talk about that, tell me about the catgut.
Well, they take the cat's gut and stretch it and let it dry out and then cut it and make a string and that's where the catgut strings --
And that's what catgut is.
Yeah. Now they may have something else to substitute it these days.
Like nylon or something, yeah.
Maybe so. I imagine so.
But that's what was used on the fiddles, was catgut?
That's right, yeah. Stretches the gut, let it dry up and then they put it on the fiddle.
And you said that from the cedar tree, they take out the wood and they make the neck of the fiddle.
Yeah, I think it's the cedar tree. One they could dry.
And they drill holes --
Yeah, they drill holes and make a neck.
Yeah.
And they'd cut it. Because the guys (inaudible) five or six guys out West -- I don't know if you
know it or not -- they set out there and they carved out many things, just sitting there talking.
(Laughter.)

(Inaudible) carve out and they're still doing that, too, in some places like Dodge City, because I go (inaudible). They're not like they are in the movie anymore, dress nice and they wear their guns inside, you know. Everybody still carries a gun, but they carry knives and they whittle. Anybody you see sitting in the street, they always whittling with knives, making things. So they carve out and they make those fiddles.
And they make the pegs?
For the fiddle?
Yeah.
Make everything, made everything.
Amazing.
Make their own fiddle bow.
Oh, they make the bow?
Yeah, they make the bow and then they (inaudible) --
Do they use catgut on the bow?
No, they go get horse's hair from his tail.
Oh, for heaven sake. Is that right?
That's what's in the fiddle bow today is horse's tail.
Is it?
Yeah, that's what's in there. They get horse's hair.
Well, I'll be darned. Fancy that.
Sure, and then they put rosin on it and they'd get the rosin from the tree, big trees out there, rosin falls out of some of the rosin trees. You knew that, didn't you?
Yeah, I think I did know that.
They get the rosin and go out there and find that rosin.
It's like the tree leaks or or something.
(Inaudible) rosin.
Well, I'll be --
Dry it out and they (inaudible). That's what happened with the fiddle set-up.
For heavens sake. Isn't that amazing.
We weren't the only ones doing that. All of them was doing it.
(Laughter.)
Yeah.
All of them. Everybody.
Well, listen, let's --
In later years, (inaudible) fiddle, just guys come over and see the fiddle Mr. Durham got. "Fiddle, man, real fiddle."
(Laughter.)
No kidding.
But they'd take cigar boxes and make fiddles all the time.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, they took cigar boxes for guitars sometimes, too, didn't they?
That's what I heard.
You never saw it, huh?
No, (inaudible) too small up there.
Yeah. Well, Eddie, listen, tell me more about your father. Tell me about -- you said he was a drinking man. He was a gambling man, you said.
Yeah, great gambler.
He was a great gambler?
Yeah, all those fellas, they gamble all the time.
Well, you told me that if he needed some change, what would he do in the morning you said?

Well, he had one of those riding saddles, because he'd put his regular saddle on the horse and then sometime he'd use that saddle on his horse to get that -- take it off his horse. But most of the times, he -- that saddle -- he
wouldn't use that saddle to ride on the horse. That was -- He'd ride bareback?
No, he'd have another saddle he'd ride his horse with. But that was a special saddle he'd use to put on one of them other horses.
Oh.
They'd rope a horse (inaudible).
So in other words, he went out to --
-- throw a saddle on. They let you throw a saddle on them.
Oh, they will?

Some of them will. Some of them try to buck. But they tie them up, feet and all, rope him up so he can't move and they'd put a saddle on him and then (inaudible) get on it. Most of them let you put a saddle on them. Some of them don't like it, but a saddle ain't big. They don't like a man on top of them.
No. Well, listen, we didn't make it really clear. What you told me was that if he needed $25, he'd go out to what? To a ranch?
Yeah, he'd go to another ranch. He knew everybody --
And say to them?
'Mr. So and So, you got a horse I can break this morning?' 'Oh, here's Joe Durham. Yeah, yeah, the
bronco, yeah."
And show him what the horse looked like?
He'd show him the horse and (inaudible) may be two days before he could catch that horse sometime.
(Laughter.)
Oh, really?
(Inaudible) wanted that money.
(Laughter.)
He'd ride that horse down the road and (inaudible).
And would he come in riding that?
No, he wouldn't come in riding the horse. But he'd lead the horse in, huh?
He'd lead him in and bring him in the corral and ride him.
No kidding.
Lead him in, bring (inaudible).
So you said you never saw your father thrown off a horse.
Never seen him get throwed. I saw guys -- they rode at least 20 horses during one show in the --
Yeah, in the -- yeah, in the rodeos.
That was one act. For a half hour, they'd ride horse right after another. (Inaudible) 80 guys standing in line. They'd get on this horse and ride and they'd

buck. People would see that. But if the guy didn't get throwed -- most of the times, they'd throw them ten feet over. They'd throw them guys off of them horses. And you didn't get throwed off, you'd have to jump off. They'd pull him off if that horse started breaking a little bit. Most of the time they threw them off, threw the guys off of them.
Yeah, because you mean, if you stay on a horse, he's no longer a bronco.
Oh, if you ever stay on him (inaudible), he's broke.
Yeah.
See, he wouldn't be no good for the show next day.
No. Eddie, did your father really ride in any of those rodeos?
Yeah, he'd ride in some of the rodeos. I didn't see him ride in the rodeos. Not racing, but he was a jockey. He was a jockey, too, with the trotters and the pacers.
Oh, he was?
Yeah, he was a jobkey.
Well, what did they use for behind them? A little --
A carriage, like they got out here (inaudible), two wheels.
No kidding. Two-wheeled carriages.

Yeah, and if the carriage break down, those guys, they'd come in (inaudible) -- (Laughter.) But, you know, that's what they used to say. The guys -- but they got them carriages like they got out here at Goshen (PHONETIC).
No kidding, at Goshen.
Yeah, they had the races -- see, they have all the preliminary races there before the big race at Monticello. (Inaudible).
Do you ever -- does Stanley Dancer come in there, because he's the big guy for that, isn't he?
Yeah, (inaudible).
Not (inaudible), Stanley Dancer. Isn't that right?
Yeah, every time I mention him, they think I'm talking about the race horse. (Laughter.)
That's funny, isn't it?
Yeah. They got pictures out there (inaudible) of all the horses that was top horses. All the horses (inaudible).
Well, did you learn to ride?
Oh yeah, I could ride.
How did you kids ride? What did you -- that's another thing you said. You know, you said your dad was a farmer, a sharecropper.
(Inaudible) horses.
From ponies?
They call them pony horses.
What are they?
They broke. They small horses like the Indians ride.
Oh.

And they broke and they train them, you know, (inaudible). And if I'd get on the horse, and he's a cow horse and you don't know how to ride him, he'd throw you right off, because when you start off -- like, if he goes right after a cow, see? And like you get on him and there's a cow out there, he goes after that cow and that's the way they round up the cows.
And they call them a cow horse?
Pony horses, yeah. Pony horses.
Pony horses, fancy that.
And they'd train them to bring in the cows. They'd turn themselves -- they'd turn every way that the cow turned. He'd turn right in front of him.
Really?
If the cow turn around like, then he'd
turn around.
(Laughter.)
: Fancy --
(Inaudible) that, but those cowboys know all that, see? They ride and then they keep -- you know, they know how they're going to turn.
: Yeah.
And when he gets ready to rope, you run him straight and when you rope that horse, as soon as that rope hits that ______, he'd tighten and rope that (inaudible).
: Yeah. This is the wild horse.
No, that's the pony horse that's trained.
: Oh.
When they rope a cow and run him down (inaudible) --
: Yeah, I see.
-- horse pulls back?
: Yeah, of course. I see.
You hook it around the horn and they rope the horse and they hook it around the horn. The horse pull and he'll jump off the horse and the horse will keep that slack on that rope though.
: Really?
Yeah and they run down the rope and grab the (inaudible) because everybody that roped a steer in
the show, (inaudible) -- Yeah.
-- then he's got to pin that steer down to -- down on the ground.
Yeah, yeah.
Then he lets the steer up.
And these are pony horses that they used to do that?
They'd use pony horses, you know.
Is that right? Fancy that.
And they trained and they go after a cow, you run right upside him (inaudible) and he'd turn his head, you know, (inaudible).
Take your hand --
Oh.
No, I mean --
Oh, yeah.
(Laughter.)

Well, listen, -- well, let's talk a minute more about your father. Like you're saying -- so, the whole family turned out to be musical and it all comes from that side of the family. Now, you did talk a little bit about this with Stan, but -- so there were four sons that were all musical and two cousins that were brought up in the family, too.
And when Battles came in, that was seven
of us. That's a pretty good-sized band. Well, did Battles -- what was he? A neighbor or what?
Yeah, when he lived with us, he was very young.
Oh, he did live with you? I didn't realize that. I know Stanley must have already said that. So that made seven of you.
That's right.

So you were about -- well, it's about time for us to start talking about -- I asked you how you got your training and you were telling me about your oldest brother Joe and you dumbfounded me by telling me that Joe was -- had joined up with Teddy Roosevelt's Rough Riders.
Yeah, he was there.
And he was with them -- you said he was with them about four years.
Somewhere around in there. Yeah, he was young when he got (inaudible) Army and he stayed in until that last war. He was in that last war.
'That last war.' That must be the Mexican-American War, I suppose. What? The last battle or something?
(Inaudible) but I can't think of the name of that guy. They had Poncho Villa and there was another
one or was he the last guy?
Well, I --
(Inaudible). Poncho Villa.
Yeah, I think that's --
Yeah, I used to know the name well.
It wasn't Zapata, was it?
No, I think it was Poncho Villa.
Yeah, yeah.
And that's when they was fighting across the border.
Yeah. Well, that's good. That's very interesting. Oh, well, listen. So then you said that he took while he was in the Army. He got all kind of good musical training.
Sure.
And he learned to -- everything -- read and --
And then when he came out of the Army, then he really -- he kept books and he stayed deep into the music and then I was deep into getting experience from what I got off of him.
Well, you said that when you were about eight years old, you visited him and that he would give you your instruction.
(Inaudible).
: What did we say? Camp Travis?
Yeah, I forgot -- that's in San Anton, isn't it?
: Is it? Well, I don't know.
Somewhere around there.
: Yeah.
Because they went from camp to camp. A lot of times they was stationed in other camps.
: Yeah. And --
And then they moved the tenth cavalry -- moved to Kansas.
: Yeah.
When I was at Kansas City in the 27 -- 1927, I didn't tell him -- I went out to see the old soldiers that my brother used to be with.
: No kidding.
A lot of old soldiers was there and they'd put on exhibitions.
: Yeah.
But they didn't allow them to have bullets.
: Oh, I see.
(Inaudible).
(Laughter.)
And the guys said (inaudible), they wouldn't give them
anymore guns (inaudible) bullets.
(Laughter.)
Really? No kidding.
They'd put on those exhibitions because anybody in the tenth cavalry on a horse could hit his target falling.
Honestly?
That's the way they'd practice. You ride the horse and you got to fall off the horse and you got to hit your target while you're falling.
Well, I never. Well, tell me --
(Inaudible) guys, if you shoot him off his horse, he'd kill you if he hadn't hit the ground.
Oh.
(Inaudible) tenth cavalry.
Well, you told me that your brother Joe taught you to shoot.
Yeah, he taught me to shoot.
You said he taught you to use a rifle?
Rifle, (inaudible), but he always (inaudible) learned to use a rifle better --
(End of Side Six.)
THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Oral History -- Eddie Durham
Sides 7 - 8

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
A little voodoo.
You think so.
Well, I don't know. Well, listen --

I had two or three of them in a box. They come by sets, see. When (inaudible) and after he gets past ________, he adds rattlers, and that's what they take, they sound, and you take them out, and they're dead in that shoebox. But after you dry them out, zoom you can hear that sound.
So then they use them in the rear fiddles, too.
They did.
They'd use them now, but there ain't not rattlers around.
Well, let's go back to Joe. You said Joe, I don't think Stanley got all this from you. You said he was a wonderful bass players.
Yep.
He had other instruments.

Yeah, he was a trumpet player. He played trumpet with ________ with the dramatic show and with the minstrel and we played -- he played trumpet with the band. and Batts played first trumpet and he played second trumpet.
With which band.
With any band, we were all together, the Durham Brothers and the Dixie Ramblers.
Battle --

I think he played trumpet -- I don't know whether he played trumpet with Calloway, I think he played bass only over there. He was with Jap Allen's band, too, played trumpet. He used to play all the instruments.
And he also knew how to --
Played violin, too.
He also knew how to write, didn't he?
Oh, yeah.
I mean, he taught you quite a little bit about it, didn't he.
Then you said that he -- when he came back home, you said that he was the one that was kind of instrumental with all the rest of you to inspire everybody to study and
He'd keep on you.
Keep on you, would he?
Yeah, to learn the music, instead of so much playing.
Yes, be serious.
He said you should read.
So he bought you your one instrument and you bought yourself the other.
Yeah.
Which did he buy you?
He got the trombone and Doug Morgan bought me a when I was on the show.
What show, the minstrel show?

No, on the dramatic show. Night show, terrific show. We had the band on there. And Battle was on there, and I think the Dixie Ramblers were involved (inaudible). But all the (inaudible) were with the Mamie Smith show.
Well, listen, all the brothers were on the Mamie Smith show.
Yep, all three brothers.
You and the other three brothers.
Yes.
What about the cousins. They had left home.

Allen went with Gene Coy's Black Aces -- wait a minute, Clyde went with Gene Coy's Black Aces and then Allen went, you know, Oklahoma City and Battles went. Then when the Mamie Smith show closed, I went to Oklahoma with Battle and got with Gene Coy's Black Aces too.
No kidding.
When we left there, formed another band, and we were all getting back together again. Sometime
one would be away.
But you had that nucleus and you'd join each other.
Yeah, we'd all get together.

Listen, while we're just thinking. I just try to remember things as they come back in my mind. I thought that was kind of touching, what you said about the cousins. Well, first of all you said everybody drank. You said practically everyone in the family did some drinking.
The two cousins drink themselves to death.
What. The two cousins did drink themselves to death.

Sure, Allen was drinking so. In '48 I went to California and he was playing and had just left Lionel Hampton, and they gave him a job in Chicago as a D.J. and he wrote me out here -- now, this is late -- that was in '48.
Now, wait a minute, what was his instrument.
Trombone.
And he was with Lionel.
Lionel Hampton, played with Lionel Hampton, Allen Barry (phonetic). Kind of light complected boy, very nice looking boy, had that old drinking look though.
That old drinking look, and he went out to the West Coast and then they brought him to Chicago.

Yeah, and then he went to the West Coast and when I was out there with the Ink Spots he was out there and a lot of people say, man, Allen still playing but he drinking. He's drinking so much. I went down to see him, yeah, yeah, I'm going to quit. I'm going to quit, yeah, I know. Make me sick. I ain't going to drink no more, I'm going to quit, but he didn't. He went to Chicago and he wrote me and the next thing I heard, the wine killed him.

And then the other brother, he started drinking because it was so close, they favored each other -- Clyde, the oldest one, they say he died six months after, grieved himself to death. Started drinking heavy too. He drank whiskey.
What was his instrument, Clyde's
Bass. That's all he ever played, was the bass fiddle. Bass horn, I meant to say.
Oh, the bass horn, the tuba you mean.
The tuba, that's what he played.
Who did he play with.

He played with Gene Coy's Black Aces and he stayed with them a lot of years, I guess, and Gene Coy. That's the same, Gene Coy's Black Aces and he might have played with somebody else and then he played with us.
I see. Well, just on the subject of the guys in the family that drink or did drink, what did you say about your own brother in Hartford.
I went and got him when Basie came in town. Said he was out and he told Macio to go get me because his brother ain't the same.
Well, wait a minute, which brother was it.
That was Earl and he was the leader of the band.
And he had a band up in Hartford and they said he was the king of the saxophone up there.

And clarinet. That's right, nobody could challenge him on that tenor. And the clarinet. I said, oh, Macio, I'll go right over there, so about three days later I went to Hartford and got him. And I said, where's your baritone -- he played them all -- somebody said, oh, he put that in pawn. Where's his tenor. He pawned that too. Where, he ain't got no ticket.

And he was sick from that drinking, I brought him to Newark by my sister, where she was living and mother and we wouldn't let him do anything. We kept him there and finally put him -- doctor and got him in the hospital and he got all right. Stayed all right for quite awhile.
How quite awhile.
Like two years.
Did he really?
Then he went back drinking again, slipping, and he got sick again. Couldn't keep him off it, he just died about five years ago. 70-something.

I went and got him and carried him to my home and he would still slip out and get that wine and he was getting his old-age pension, that's what the trouble was. I went down and tried to stop them from sending him money, just keep your money, and they still would send it.
But I think the investigators had a lot to do with that because they would bring it to him.
They would bring it to him.

Yeah, they would get it for him and like that and they would rip him off of that money by getting him some whiskey, so when he was at my house in Brooklyn -- I got a place over there now -- I left him there one night, and I went to play downtown and the house caught on fire because he had went out and he went to sleep before I left -- the wife and kids went out and he went back in the room (inaudible) trying to keep him there, but that money he could get up and go to the city and get that money, still kept the same address.
But he was on the seventh floor of a hotel on relief and if the place ever caught on fire, he'd never get out. The sprinkling system didn't even reach that seventh floor. I
told him I'd come over and get his money and don't give it to him (inaudible) and they'd give it to him, just throw away money.

So that's what happened to him. The house caught on fire, he had set the house on fire, with a cigarette and the firemen got there and he run outside and the fire -- I was just coming (inaudible) he was saying, I don't know that refrigerator must have set it on fire. I said, well, what about this in your back pocket here. Oh, I just went and gothat. I just went and got it while you (inaudible) so he got away with it. About three apartments went out on the first floor, three rooms.
Was that a dead loss for you or did your insurance cover part.
Dead loss. I made a little profit because I'm a good carpenter and I built it back the way I wanted it.
No kidding, that's great.

Made money and had some left. I knew the insurance broker. I knew the bank so well and I had a mortgage with them. He said you do the job the way you want it, I've known you so long. I put every decoration I really wanted to put in there.
Well, listen, Eddie, let's go back now because we didn't talk about how when your brother came
back and there was like seven of you with all the different instruments, so you said people would call you up and contact you to play different jobs, weddings and things like that.
Oh, yes, jobs just like they're hustling gigs now.
Yes, so the whole family would go out on the jobs.
Yeah, we'd get them through the school.
And then you said there was a guy, you said, was like an older guy and he was the drummer and he would be the contractor.
With Kansas City -- with one of the teams in Texas.
Oh, he was a baseball player.
Yes, a professional. Those guys were terrific.
This was the black leagues.
Yeah, and he played with the Pittsburgh -- you know, they had a lot of teams around, I forget the name of them now, Kansas City Monarchs, -- that was Satchel Paige's team.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: Copyright notice and Smithsonian interview header
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warning and the Smithsonian oral history title page: interviewer Stanley Dance, Washington, August 1978.

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: Sound test and Durham's birth date and place
segments.summary: After a sound check, Durham gives his birth as 19 August 1909 in San Marcos, Texas, though books say 1906.

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: San Marcos, Texas, and his father the farmer and fiddler
segments.summary: San Marcos was a small farming and cattle town with many Spanish speakers; his father farmed, broke broncos and played fiddle for dances.

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: Mother, brothers and cousins who played music
segments.summary: His mother was not musical but his brothers Joe, Earl and Roosevelt and cousins Clyde and Allen all played; he sorts out the birth order and instruments.

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: The family band and learning trombone and guitar from Joe
segments.summary: The family played weekend gigs without a drummer; oldest brother Joe, stationed with the 24th Infantry near Teddy Roosevelt's guard, taught him trombone and guitar.

segments.chapter: Opening and Texas childhood
segments.title: The 1927 photograph with Battles and nine instruments
segments.summary: Durham describes a picture dated 1927 with Battles showing banjo, four-string guitar and trombone, three men playing nine instruments.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Doug Morgan's Dramatic Show and his first guitar
segments.summary: His first professional travel was with Doug Morgan's dramatic show, a white show with a black band, where he got his first guitar and played trombone.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: What the 101 Ranch show was like
segments.summary: He describes the 101 Ranch Wild West circus with Indian tribes, staged raids, a big arena and its last show at Yankee Stadium.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Two seasons with the 101 Ranch
segments.summary: He stayed two warm-weather seasons, touring all over the States.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: The white parade band and the black minstrel band
segments.summary: The show had a big white parade band and a 14-15 piece black band that was cut to nine for the night minstrel show.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Learning to voice four- and five-part harmony
segments.summary: Playing trombone and guitar in the band and giving dances afterwards, he experimented with voicing four trombones above the usual triads.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Setting the circus band up as an orchestra
segments.summary: He explains trombones in early jazz, his use of bass drum and trap drummers, French horns for piano sound and clarinets for reeds, and the band's size.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: March books, minstrel repertoire and the blues that turned the tide
segments.summary: The band played ragtime and march books until Durham's blues from the wagon changed it; he left the circus around 1921 at Yankee Stadium.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Black band musicians and the circus going to Europe
segments.summary: Uncertain whether the black band went to Europe; he names trumpeters Amos White and John Mason and a fine drummer.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Hearing Louis Armstrong with King Oliver in Chicago
segments.summary: He heard Armstrong with King Oliver in a Chicago ballroom, listening at the windows, then worked at Starkey's Bakery and studied with the U.S. School of Music.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Circus pay of about $25 a week
segments.summary: The 101 Ranch paid around $25 a week with room and board, good money; others earned $40-50 and he saved in the bank.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: A year or two in Chicago, then Kansas City
segments.summary: He stayed in Chicago about a year or two before going into the business seriously in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Circus wagons, horses, elephants and moving the show
segments.summary: Band wagons were horse-drawn, an elephant called Big Jimbo pushed stuck wagons, the show travelled on its own trains; Durham wrote jazz licks for the minstrel wagon.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Six-part harmony and conflict in the Bennie Moten band
segments.summary: Joining Moten, he used the harmony learned in the circus; the band resisted the sixth, Lips Page played it, Moten said to play what he wrote, and he played valve trombone.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Mamie Smith's 7-11 show and Battles' band
segments.summary: After the 101 he went with the Goldberg Brothers' 7-11 show with Mamie Smith in a nine-piece band led by Edgar Battle with Herschel Evans; he wrote what the band could play.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Playing the pit for the show with his brothers
segments.summary: The band played the overture and show in the pit and had to read; Joe, Earl, Roosevelt and Eddie were all in the band, but only Joe was in the 101.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Dating Mamie Smith and the Chicago stay
segments.summary: They try to date the Mamie Smith show to about 1921 and work out whether Chicago came before it.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: The Chicago trade school and learning from Don Redman in New York
segments.summary: He lived with Dr. Dorsey, worked at the lunch counter, learned musical terms at school, then in New York met Bingie Madison and Don Redman's six-part harmony.

segments.chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
segments.title: Bands not ready for rich voicings
segments.summary: Bands could not read or hear anything beyond triads, though he wrote six-sax voicings for Battles.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Hiding odd notes in Basie's reed section; Ellington, Redman and Kenton
segments.summary: Durham used organ harmony and flat fifths in Basie's reeds without writing accidentals; he compares Ellington, Redman and Kenton as creators who go out in space.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Between the Battle show and Moten: Kansas City, Oklahoma bands, Blue Devils
segments.summary: Asked what came next, he lists Gene Coy, Jesse Stone, Terrence Holder and Walter Page's Blue Devils, each only for weeks, before joining Moten.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Gene Coy's Black Aces in Oklahoma
segments.summary: Gene Coy's band played the Blue Glass Ballroom in Oklahoma, with his cousins Allen on trombone and Clyde on bass getting him in.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Chauncey Downs' Rinky Dinks and the brass clique
segments.summary: In Kansas City he played with front man Chauncey Downs' band, forming a brass clique with Eddie Tompkins, Paul Webster and Keg Johnson, who all moved to Jesse Stone.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Jesse Stone as arranger and bandleader
segments.summary: They liked Jesse Stone because he threw anything on paper; Durham calls him underrated, ten years ahead, and describes him now playing organ with his wife.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Terrence Holder and Andy Kirk takes over the band
segments.summary: Durham was with Holder's band only a few weeks before Holder ran off, apparently with the money, and Andy Kirk was given the band.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: How cooperative bands split the money
segments.summary: Territory bands were cooperative: Moten rented halls, paid expenses, and divided the take equally, believing sidemen were worth as much as the leader.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Joining the Blue Devils through Buster Smith and Booker Pittman
segments.summary: He knew Buster Smith and Booker Pittman from the Blue Moon Chasers and moved on to the Blue Devils when he got hungry.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Where the names Blue Devils, Clouds of Joy and Black Aces came from
segments.summary: They speculate on the name Blue Devils (Ellison's range-war story, blues as depression) and Durham's view that names identified black bands.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Meeting Buster Smith in Dallas and the Texas music school
segments.summary: He met Buster Smith in Dallas while at a music school under Professor Barnett, played dances with his band, and calls Smith self-taught and the greatest.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Buster Smith and the One O'Clock Jump
segments.summary: Smith brought a trunk of blues music for the Kansas City story; Durham says Smith really did One O'Clock Jump and he and Dan added the trombone parts, earning the nickname Circus Boy.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Buster Smith's reluctance to travel and his recent playing
segments.summary: Smith won't fly and is superstitious; Durham describes seeing him at the Kansas City concert and a Decca record they made together.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Buster Smith teaching Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Durham recalls Smith showing young Charlie Parker how to hold the alto, Parker's poor tone, and Parker trying to play like Smith until finding his own style.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Parker's tone and why black players' tones blend badly in sections
segments.summary: Smith disliked Parker's tone, which would not blend; Durham says white players use one or two tones while black players have many, making section fit harder.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Lester Young's tone and how Durham voiced him in the Basie saxophones
segments.summary: Lester's whispery tone was bad against Hawkins' sound, so Durham wrote him high on the C melody part next to the second alto, never on the root.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Who led the Blue Devils
segments.summary: Walter Page led the Blue Devils, though Durham thinks someone else may earlier have led.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Walter Page playing bass on baritone sax
segments.summary: Page played bass lines on baritone sax in the Blue Devils, easier to carry than a string bass, and Durham wanted that in Moten's band.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Writing the baritone with the bass in arrangements
segments.summary: Durham sometimes wrote the baritone with the bass, as in Lunceford's band and Running a Temperature, for heavy reed tone in the bass section.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Poor bass amplification, rock and conga drums
segments.summary: Early amplification lost the bass in crowded halls; he thinks this helped rock take over and that rhythm sections were too small for big bands.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Blue Devils personnel and why it broke up
segments.summary: He lists Lips Page, Walter Page, Buster Smith, Dan Minor, Alvin Burroughs and Jimmy Rushing; the money was light so he left for Moten.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Blue Devils musicians join Moten and the band grows
segments.summary: Many Blue Devils joined Moten for big pay; the brass grew from three to six, reeds from three to four, and the banjo gave way to guitar and Freddie Green.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Walter Page's bass tone and Gene Ramey
segments.summary: Page's strength and big hands made the stage sway; Durham compares the big-toned bassists of the time and praises Gene Ramey.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: The Kansas City rhythm section with Buster Smith
segments.summary: For the Kansas City concert Durham played guitar with Smith on piano, Gene Ramey and Joe Jones, which he says amazed listeners.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: Bringing Buster Smith to New York and Durham's busy life
segments.summary: He plans to bring Smith to play at his gig, describes Smith's family life, and mentions being busy with his kids' property and Battle's dying.

segments.chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
segments.title: His current small-group scoring and organ voicings
segments.summary: He is writing for about eight pieces like the Kansas City Six, and plays tenor trombone, drums, piano and organ in a tightly arranged quartet.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Joining Moten: guitar and trombone, arranging from the start
segments.summary: With Moten he alternated trombone and guitar, mostly soloing on guitar, and began arranging immediately; Basie came in about the same time.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: The new Moten band's records and Durham as sole arranger
segments.summary: He says Lafayette, Toby and similar numbers were his, with Barefield contributing, and no one else was writing for the band.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Head arrangements, Herschel Evans' ear and Lester Young's reading
segments.summary: Moten could not head, but with Basie riffs Durham wrote leads and Herschel Evans harmonized by ear; Lester read well but needed time.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: The 1929 band and which Moten numbers he arranged
segments.summary: They check the 1929 personnel and the 1932 session, and Durham lists the titles he arranged, such as New Vine Street Blues and Mary Lee.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: How Basie became Count
segments.summary: Moten kept saying Basie was no account for leaving arrangements unfinished, so Durham wrote a tune called The Count.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Moten as a pianist and the 1929 versus 1932 recordings
segments.summary: Moten read anything and played well only with music in front of him; the 1932 sides began to swing more.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Identifying his arrangements on the 1932 records
segments.summary: Durham recalls Blue Room, Lafayette, New Orleans and Prince of Wales as his and says he must hear the records to be sure.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Walking chromatic bass lines and band resistance
segments.summary: Players resisted his chromatic walking bass in One O'Clock Jump and his new style until the record came out and was accepted.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Influences: Ellington and Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Durham says Ellington influenced him most, with Henderson keeping jazz as dance music, and he now sees Ellington as 50 years ahead.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Ellington versus Strayhorn
segments.summary: They compare Strayhorn's trained, nearly white style with Ellington's self-acquired music, and agree Ellington was untouchable and produced more after Strayhorn died.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Homemade amplified guitar and the clothes-hanger bridge
segments.summary: Durham explains rigging an amplifier and mike to his guitar and a clothes-hanger swinging bridge, a few years before factory electric guitars.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Resonator guitar and acoustic guitar on Honey Keep Your Mind on Me
segments.summary: Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me was acoustic; earlier he used a resonator guitar with a tin piece and mike, giving a bottle-like electrified sound.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: First electric guitar on the Kansas City Six sides
segments.summary: His first electric guitar came with Bon Bon's Buddies and the Kansas City Six on Hello Little Girl, though instruments were poor then.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Teaching Charlie Christian the downstroke in Oklahoma City
segments.summary: In 1937 Durham showed Christian in a pool hall how to play single-note downstrokes like a horn, and Christian picked it up in minutes.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Hearing T-Bone Walker with an electric guitar
segments.summary: He heard T-Bone Walker in the mid 1930s in the South, a showman with an electric guitar playing terrific blues.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: The Seattle amplifier story and the guitar players' hour off
segments.summary: In Seattle, probably 1938, guitar players were given an hour off to hear him with his amplifier, and his amp failed on stage.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Makers of amplified and resonator guitars
segments.summary: He names Ampliphone, Gibson, Stella and National resonators and describes the odd sound he got on Battles' records.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Floyd Smith and Floyd's Guitar Blues
segments.summary: He talked Floyd Smith's mother into buying him a $70 guitar in Nebraska; Smith later made the commercial Floyd's Guitar Blues with Andy Kirk.

segments.chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
segments.title: Steel guitar and T-Bone Walker's style
segments.summary: Smith used a steel guitar; Durham says T-Bone Walker was early, with gimmicks, strong bass strings and a jazzy blues swing.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Leaving Moten and going to New York to Willie Bryant
segments.summary: He left four weeks before Moten died, wanting something bigger, and went to New York at Bryant's request, where union transfer rules limited his playing.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Sides 3-4, Washington, November 1978
segments.summary: Header for the second Smithsonian session in November 1978.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Joining Willie Bryant as an arranger because of the union
segments.summary: Willie Bryant's band recommended him; he was made an arranger since the union barred him from playing, and he stayed about six months with Benny Carter, Cozy Cole and Teddy Wilson.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Chimes in the Chapel and the Bryant personnel
segments.summary: He recalls writing Chimes in the Chapel for Bryant and works through the saxophone and trumpet sections with Lorenzo Pack, Johnny Russell, Battles and Richard Clark.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Willie Bryant as singer and mayor of Harlem
segments.summary: Bryant sang most numbers, having no instrument; Durham says he was called mayor of Harlem and carried a gold pistol.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Union transfer waiting periods
segments.summary: Durham explains the six-month wait for new members in New York, how transfers work now, and his membership in four locals at once.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: The three clique and Lunceford's pursuit
segments.summary: Lunceford tried for about four years to hire him through the Kansas City trio of Tompkins, Webster and Durham, who studied during school years.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Tompkins and Webster's school escapades and hearing Lunceford at the Parlor
segments.summary: Webster and Tompkins joined Lunceford in summers; Durham heard the band at the Parlor, found it a show band, and joined at $35 a week.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: The Lunceford style and teaching six-part harmony
segments.summary: Lunceford was a novelty band with dancers, glee club and trio; Durham voiced six-part harmony for a five-horn section and left because pay stopped at $60-65.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Lunceford's finances, Hammond and the move back to Basie
segments.summary: When the band's corporation ended and pay was cut, John Hammond told him Basie needed arrangements, and Basie offered $75 for playing and $75 for arranging.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Durham's Lunceford arrangements
segments.summary: He lists Harlem Shout, Lunceford Special, Bird of Paradise, Running a Temperature, Hitting the Bottle and Avalon, and contrasts his writing with Sy Oliver's.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Lunceford's sax section, Willie Smith and Jimmy Crawford's two-beat
segments.summary: Willie Smith played so loudly that nothing was written for the reeds, and drummer Jimmy Crawford's two-beat style defined the band.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Why he left Lunceford
segments.summary: Trummy Young took his place; he left for money and gives the dates as early 1935 to 1937.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: The Basie versus Lunceford battle of the bands in Hartford
segments.summary: He switched bands the night of a Hartford battle of the bands and was interviewed on radio, praising both bands.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Whether Lunceford swung and Sy Oliver's band today
segments.summary: Durham calls Lunceford a novelty band with a two-beat that suited dancers and praises Sy Oliver's small band for staying working.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Returning to Basie and never opening his book
segments.summary: Going back to Basie was easy because he remembered the books and never pulled one out in Lunceford's band either.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Dickie Wells replaces him at the Shady Rest
segments.summary: At the Shady Rest in Newark Dickie Wells came up with Durham's book and took his trombone chair; Durham stayed one year with Basie.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Why he left Basie and Basie's reluctance to play new arrangements
segments.summary: Durham found Basie more interested in a good time than business or writing; Basie avoided odd arrangements, so Durham pushed Buck Clayton's charts.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Writing Topsy on the train to Albany
segments.summary: Rejoining the band, he wrote Topsy on the train to Albany and prepared a rough score so Harry Edison and others could read it at rehearsal.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Wham and giving Glenn Miller half the credit
segments.summary: Wham was written for Moten, reworked for lyricist Taps Miller, and recorded by Glenn Miller in exchange for half the writer credit.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: Sharing composer credit to get songs recorded
segments.summary: Durham argues that giving half a song to a big name was worth it, discussing Fats Waller, Hodges and Ellington and the obstacles for black writers.

segments.chapter: Bryant, Lunceford and Basie
segments.title: John's Idea and Hammond's tribute
segments.summary: Durham says he named John's Idea after Hammond, who did not credit him at the tribute night.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: What made Kansas City riffs distinctive
segments.summary: Kansas City riffs always carried a melody you could build a song from, like Moten Swing and Lester Young's riffs.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Tempo in Kansas City jazz, Basie and Jo Jones
segments.summary: Basie and Jo Jones were masters of the right dance tempo, as in Moten Swing and One O'Clock Jump, and Durham says tempo makes a hit.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire
segments.summary: Harlan Leonard's too-fast version failed, while Tommy Tucker's number-one hit of Durham's song with Benny Benjamin used the right tempo.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Jay McShan's Kansas City feel
segments.summary: Durham praises McShan's tempo sense and riffs as underrated, comparing him on piano to T-Bone Walker on guitar.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Writing down Until the Real Thing Comes Along on the riverbank
segments.summary: Dancers Pha Terrell and Van hummed the song to him at 3 a.m. and he notated it, took no credit, and later lost the manuscript.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Kansas City singers and pianists
segments.summary: They discuss Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, Julia Lee, other Kansas City singers and pianists, and Juanita Bolo.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Years in Kansas City and its around-the-clock nightlife
segments.summary: He was in Kansas City from 1927 to the early 1930s; clubs and liquor stores never closed under the Pendergast regime.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: After hours at 18th and Vine and with Joe Turner
segments.summary: Musicians met in the street at 18th and Vine and Durham played after hours with Joe Turner and Jo Jones, paid in money stuffed in his guitar.

segments.chapter: Kansas City style and nightlife
segments.title: Ben Webster in the streetcar tracks
segments.summary: Ben Webster would stand drinking wine in the middle of the streetcar tracks and dodge the cops.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Arranging Them There Eyes for Artie Shaw and Billie Holiday
segments.summary: After Basie he arranged for Ina Ray Hutton, Glenn Miller and Artie Shaw, writing Them There Eyes for Billie Holiday.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Touring with Ina Ray Hutton's all-woman band
segments.summary: He traveled with Hutton's band for a year, hand-picked musicians, imported a British first trumpeter, and wrote for a ten-week Chicago broadcast.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Ina Ray Hutton's band in a battle of the bands with Dick Jurgens
segments.summary: At Madison Square Garden the girls copied Basie's One O'Clock Jump as a gag, and in Chicago Durham made a double band with Dick Jurgens' players.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Why the girls' band drew crowds and the Paramount opening
segments.summary: The band was favored for being women, opened at the Paramount, previewed in Rochester, and Hutton wanted it to swing like Basie.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Arranging for Glenn Miller
segments.summary: His contract was two arrangements a week, but he rehearsed each one at length: St. Louis Blues, In the Mood and Tuxedo Junction.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Declining a captain's rating when Miller went overseas
segments.summary: Miller's offer of a captain's rating and training did not suit him; he stayed about a year and a half and did not go overseas.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: His 1940 band and Bon Bon Tunnell's Buddies
segments.summary: He led a band in 1940 and was musical director for singer Bon Bon, whose wife stopped him traveling, which ended the band.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: The Oak Grove Casino band at Bridgeport
segments.summary: His band played a year at the Oak Grove Casino in Bridgeport with Freddy Webster, Buster Smith and others, earning a Walter Winchell write-up.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Politicians, racketeers and segregation trouble at the pier
segments.summary: Wires were cut on the pier, and his plan for a night for whites drew complaints of segregating from black musicians.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Taking over the International Sweethearts of Rhythm
segments.summary: He left because his bands kept being drafted, rehearsed the Sweethearts in Washington, and had them stun musicians at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Sweethearts personnel and their wealthy backer
segments.summary: Vi Burnside was the tenor star; a rich Washington backer funded two bands, sleeper buses and big acts.

segments.chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
segments.title: Eddie Durham's All-Star Girls Band and wartime travel
segments.summary: His second girls' band ran separately from the Sweethearts, mixed black and white girls, toured with Treasury Department sign-up, and lent its sleeper bus to others.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Cavalcade of Jazz with Jack Teagarden
segments.summary: On a 1947 touring package with Teagarden, Dinah Washington, Lips Page and others, Durham wrote the whole show.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: How the Cavalcade show was staged and paid
segments.summary: He wrote openers and closers for each star act; Teagarden got $1,000 a week and the printed magazine sold well at a dollar fifty.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: The rhythm and blues tour of the South
segments.summary: After the Cavalcade he led a small band with Larry Darnell and Wynonie Harris, playing crowds of 4,000-5,000 black audiences across the South.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Wynonie Harris's stage act and records
segments.summary: Harris was hard to get along with and wanted to be the whole show; Durham controlled the band and arranged Bloodshot Eyes and All She Wants to Do Is Rock.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: The House of Blues and Booze sign
segments.summary: Harris repainted a club sign to read the House of Blues and Booze, which the liquor authority disliked.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Harris's unpaid tickets, bad language and downfall
segments.summary: Harris lost his home and car, never paid tickets, was banned from broadcasts, and died in California buried by Jimmy Evans.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Chris Roustion the bass player as Harris's bouncer
segments.summary: Bassist Chris Roustion was paid extra to rouse Harris out of hotel rooms and throw him in the car.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Harris's singing power
segments.summary: Harris was the first to dance on his heels and as loud as a six-piece band when amplified; Durham played guitar in that band.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Handover to Penny and Sides 5-6 header
segments.summary: The interviewer steps out and asks about Swingers Inc. and Moby Dick's, then the Sides 5-6 header begins.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: The 1953 three-band package show with Little Richard
segments.summary: He booked and led a theater package with Little Richard's band, his own six-piece and a six-piece girl band, and trouble started when a promoter ran off with deposits.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Dancers, singers and the backers of the show
segments.summary: The show added dancers and singers including the Durmettes, with backing from a wealthy family, and he bought the Dominoes' station wagon.

segments.chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
segments.title: Stock cards, theater bookings and how the lawyer ruined it
segments.summary: The tour did percentage in theaters until his West Indian lawyer took deposit money, so he dropped the show and Little Richard moved on.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Brother Roosevelt's piano records
segments.summary: Roosevelt recorded originals on a bad piano for Battle, singing and playing like Fats Waller, and the records never came out.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Battle's recording equipment
segments.summary: Before he died Battle bought expensive recording gear, which was moved to a friend's basement.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Marriages and raising children
segments.summary: After that last big tour he married, has had three or four wives, and ended up raising the children himself.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Playing Moby Dick's on Long Island
segments.summary: He played trombone and guitar at Moby Dick's near Jones Beach with Slick Jones and his brother, a packed place that burned down.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Steady salary at Moby Dick's and the social security story
segments.summary: It was his first straight-salary job: scale plus five percent of the cash registers, and he paid the owner's social security taxes.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: The new owner's marital trouble and the fires
segments.summary: The Florida buyer's wife set the club on fire twice over his affair with the barmaid; Durham opened his own club and played nine places.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: ASCAP royalties and checking record company books
segments.summary: Royalties from Basie material and air shots were once as high as $1,700 a check, then fell as ASCAP paid new rock and roll writers; auditing record company books is hopeless.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: No money from the million-selling Part Two Topsy
segments.summary: Durham says he never got paid on the Topsy hit because of a publisher mix-up with Love Records and Cliff Records.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Edgar Battle's handling of his money
segments.summary: Battle, raised partly in Durham's family, treated Durham's money as his own and gave no statements after 1959.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Battle's career, his scored tributes and recordings
segments.summary: Battle came back from a USO tour with $60,000, bought land, wrote large-scale tributes, and recorded gospel and spirituals.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Battle's big schemes and the estate
segments.summary: Battle always wanted large sums to start and drew back from backers; the daughter and Durham consider producing his records.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: How hard Battle's records would be to sell
segments.summary: They discuss needing a hit, selling a catalog in a lump, retaining percentage rights, and producers not wanting another name on the label.

segments.chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
segments.title: Which of his songs still earn royalties
segments.summary: Topsy and I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire were his biggest, and Yesterday Here You Come Today and Wham still bring checks via MCA.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Playing the West End with Frank Williams and Phil Schaap's venue
segments.summary: Durham returned to New York about four years ago, played the West End with Frank Williams, then discusses a feud and the struggling Third Phase.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: The Orange Inn in Goshen and his band
segments.summary: He leads a group with Hal Austin at the Orange Inn in Goshen, with a tenor and clarinet player he schools and an upscale crowd.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Audience requests, A-Train and trombone showmanship
segments.summary: He plays mostly requests, closes with a standing-ovation A-Train, uses trombone gimmicks, and arranges Sweet Georgia Brown Basie-style.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Going to Europe and planning a record
segments.summary: He has been abroad only with Lunceford; he would tour Europe for exposure and wants to record with a seven-piece group, cutting to five for travel.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: How the trombone has been held back
segments.summary: Writers give trombones little; Durham says it has 14 positions, not seven, and wants to bring out more of what it can do.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Plungers, mutes and Tricky Sam
segments.summary: They compare plunger and solo-tone mutes, Duke Ellington's effects, Jack Teagarden as open-horn man and Tricky Sam Nanton.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Trombone stylists: Dorsey, Wells, Higginbotham, Trummy Young
segments.summary: Asked who set trombone styles, Durham discusses Tommy Dorsey's sweet tone, Dicky Wells, J.C. Higginbotham and Trummy Young, who he thinks was buried.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Why an arranger in a big band doesn't play
segments.summary: With Lunceford and others he wrote for others and pushed the band rather than soloing, so nobody knew he could play.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Valve trombone versus slide
segments.summary: He played valve trombone on many Moten records; valves cut notes mechanically while slide players lip between positions, as in J.J. Johnson.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: A planned three-trombone project
segments.summary: He wants to write for three B-flat trombones playing slurs, marking positions, and would try Dicky Wells.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Young trombonists who go too high
segments.summary: He and the interviewer say Bill Watrous and Phil Wilson go into the stratosphere, and nobody wants to play melody like Tommy Dorsey.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Playing slow melody on Georgia at the Kansas City concert
segments.summary: At the 16-piece Kansas City show he played Georgia and Danny Boy straight with a plunger and the house came down.

segments.chapter: The 1970s and the trombone
segments.title: Playing melody and phrasing: Hodges, Ray Charles, Parker
segments.summary: Henry's straight Misty won a standing ovation; Durham says melody phrased well wins the public, citing Hodges, Armstrong and Ray Charles, against Parker's showmanship.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Re-recording: mother, the flood and the 1910 census
segments.summary: Helen Dance restarts the lost tape; Durham recalls a flood before 1910 and a census listing parents Rabb and Joseph Durham and the children.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: How his birth year got moved
segments.summary: His brother gave wrong birth years to the draft board because his mother was too ill to testify.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Irish and Mexican grandfather, father's Spanish name, mother's Mohawk blood
segments.summary: Durham says his grandfather Durham was Irish and married a Mexican woman, his father was called Jose with a waxed mustache, and his mother had Mohawk blood.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: His long plaited hair as a boy
segments.summary: As a boy his hair was long, kept in two plaits tied with ribbons.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Touring with the Alabama and Georgia Minstrels at 16 or 17
segments.summary: When minstrel shows came through town they hired him on trombone; Edgar Battle was in the shows and trumpeter Harry White could play jazz.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: His father's appearance and the Durham family's complexions
segments.summary: His father had perfect Mexican color; the Durham boys looked Mexican and the girls were light-skinned, with relatives in California.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: His father's fiddle playing and beating time with hat pins
segments.summary: His father could fiddle for a hundred dancers from nine to one while the boys beat rhythm on the strings with hat pins.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Cigar-box fiddles and rattlesnake rattles inside them
segments.summary: Frontier fiddles were made from cigar boxes and cedar necks with dried rattlesnake rattles dropped inside for loudness; he sold rattles for 25 cents.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: How he hunted rattlesnakes
segments.summary: He explains finding rattlers under rocks, shooting them from a distance, and why the others flee a gunshot.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Catgut strings, cedar necks, horsehair bows and rosin
segments.summary: Durham describes how western fiddle makers made strings from gut, necks from cedar, bows from horse's tail hair and rosin from trees.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: His father the gambler and bronco breaker
segments.summary: His father gambled heavily and would raise money by going to ranches to break horses; Durham never saw him thrown.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: His father as a jockey and harness racing at Goshen
segments.summary: His father also rode trotters and pacers with two-wheeled carriages; Durham compares the races at Goshen and recalls Stanley Dancer.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Pony horses and roping steers
segments.summary: He explains how trained cow ponies turn with the cow and hold the rope in cattle roping and steer pinning.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Seven in the family band after Battles joined
segments.summary: Four sons and two cousins made six musicians, and Edgar Battle, who lived with the family young, made seven.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Brother Joe's army service and musical training
segments.summary: Joe served with the Tenth Cavalry, learned music in the army, and taught Durham on visits to his camp from about age eight.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Tenth Cavalry exhibitions and Joe teaching him to shoot
segments.summary: In Kansas City in 1927 he saw old Tenth Cavalry soldiers put on shooting exhibitions, hitting targets while falling; Joe taught him to use a rifle.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Sides 7-8 header
segments.summary: Smithsonian header for Sides 7-8 of the interview.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Joe's instruments, urging study and the family bands
segments.summary: Joe played trumpet, bass and violin and wrote music; he pushed his brothers to read, bought Eddie's trombone, and they played as the Durham Brothers and Dixie Ramblers.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Brothers and cousins reuniting in Mamie Smith's show and Gene Coy's band
segments.summary: All the brothers were on the Mamie Smith show and the cousins went to Gene Coy's Black Aces; Eddie later joined in Oklahoma.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Cousins Allen and Clyde drank themselves to death
segments.summary: Cousin Allen, a trombonist with Lionel Hampton, died of wine and Clyde, the tuba player, followed within months.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Brother Earl's drinking and the Brooklyn fire
segments.summary: Earl, a fine saxophonist and clarinetist, pawned his horns for drink; Durham took him in, his pension money fed his drinking, and he set Durham's house on fire.

segments.chapter: Family and Texas roots
segments.title: Family gigs and the drummer who was a Negro League ballplayer
segments.summary: The family got wedding and dance jobs through school, with an older drummer who played baseball for a Kansas City Monarchs-type team as contractor.
